title: Troubled NT university unveils new vice-chancellor following string of bungles
text:
The Northern Territory's embattled Charles Darwin University (CDU) has appointed a new vice-chancellor and president, as the institution looks to recover from a string of controversies.

CDU announced Fiona Coulson's appointment to the leadership positions this week, after she spent the past nine months filling in the role following former vice-chancellor Scott Bowman's resignation in February.

Professor Bowman stepped down after an accreditation bungle impacting hundreds of CDU TAFE students, which saw them graduate without completing essential units.

Scott Bowman resigned from the vice-chancellor position earlier this year. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Later that same week, CDU walked away from its $1.9 million decision to establish a campus in London, saying the project was no longer financially viable.

And In June, the Fair Work Ombudsman ordered the university to backpay 823 staff more than $4 million in wages.

NT's sole university to be forced to meet KPIs After a series of scandals, the NT's only university will soon be forced to prove its taxpayer funding is having positive outcomes for students.

Professor Coulson told the ABC regaining the community's trust in CDU was of paramount importance in the wake of a difficult period.

"It is regularly that we're reminded of those mistakes, and it's going to take some time to rebuild that trust," she said.

" I think you've got to be open about these things — you own up to it, you take accountability for it, you put the systems and processes in place to ensure they don't happen again. "

She said, however, the decision to establish a London campus was "the right decision at the time," and would have gone ahead were it not for CDU's financial situation.

"Changes to international student numbers changed the project's viability," she said.

CDU has been rocked by a string of bungles over 2026. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

CDU data shows as of 2025, 35 per cent of non-TAFE students at the university were international students, with international student enrolments having almost tripled over the past five years.

Professor Coulson said CDU's reliance on international students was justified.

She flagged she would be advocating for changes to the Commonwealth's student caps, saying the policy had taken a financial toll on the university.

Fiona Coulson has been at CDU since 2022. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"It is a very difficult proposition to run a university in a small population across the vast distances we do," she said.

"The reality is international students support what we do here.

" I refute that we're a visa factory. "

Job redundancies flagged amid restructure

CDU has confirmed eight administrative staff will be made redundant following an ongoing internal restructure at the university.

The ABC understands the restructure was announced to staff on October 30 and will take effect in early December.

A restructure will see some administrative roles at the university made redundant. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Professor Coulson confirmed several roles in the organisation were being "reclassified", but insisted the university was trying to find savings in vacant positions where possible.

"There are some staff that have been negatively affected by this," she said.

"We've gone through a process, and we've really tried to limit those."

Professor Coulson attributed the restructure to the downturn in international student enrolments, reiterating the financial impact of the federal government's international student caps on CDU.

title: Bikie admits to inquiry he may have charged Vic taxpayers for shifts not worked
text:
Text messages have been shown to Victoria's Big Build royal commission exposing the efforts of a CFMEU organiser to ensure a bikie was hired on a government building site.

In its seventh day of hearings, the royal commission into alleged corruption on major public projects called on current member of outlaw motorcycle gang the Bandidos and former member of the Rebels, Joel Leavitt, to give evidence.

Various text messages between Mr Leavitt and CFMEU (Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union) organiser Jerry McQuaid were read out which showed the union wanted Mr Leavitt hired as a labourer on a Big Build project in Melbourne's south-east for construction company Laing O'Rourke.

Counsel Assisting Chris Carr SC appeared frustrated at times with Mr Leavitt's lack of recollection of events. (Supplied)

The messages showed Mr McQuaid's persistence over a series of months from November 2021 and suggested Laing O'Rourke showed resistance, refusing to employ the bikie on the Cranbourne site.

In one message Mr McQuaid wrote to Mr Leavitt that the CFMEU was "pushing like f***".

In another message, Mr McQuaid said he had "been walloping them all week".

The inquiry heard when the contractor did not comply, the union launched an industrial campaign against them.

Mr McQuaid wrote in one message "Joe's abused the f*** out of them and we're all going there to play up tomorrow".

It was suggested that the company did not want to hire Mr Leavitt because of his criminal record, which included riot, affray and assault charges.

"I think I'm a pretty good worker," Mr Leavitt said.

Asked what qualities Mr Leavitt had for the CFMEU to push "incredibly hard" to have him employed on a job site, Mr Leavitt replied "I'm a good bloke".

"One possibility might be that the CFMEU wanted to go to such lengths to get you on this job site because you're an intimidating bikie," counsel assisting the commission Chris Carr SC said.

"I wouldn't have a clue, you'd have to ask them," Mr Leavitt replied.

Taxpayers possibly charged for shifts not worked

Mr Leavitt admitted it was possible he had charged taxpayers for shifts on the Cranbourne rail project when he was not at work.

The inquiry was shown some of Mr Leavitt's time sheets claiming hours of work as a health and safety representative (HSR), which did not appear to match his phone records — which showed him either at the gym or home.

At one stage, the commissioner and counsel assisting had Mr Leavitt write "HSR" six times on a piece of paper to see if it matched the handwriting on his time sheet, because he had claimed he could not recall whether or not he wrote it.

Under questioning from commissioner Chris Kourakis, Mr Leavitt said he could not remember seeking payments for hours that did not match his phone record.

Mr Leavitt: There is potential that that could have happened. I can't recall to that time. Mr Kourakis: What you recall about the man you were back then, was that you wouldn't rule out and you can't rule out that you claimed for hours you didn't work? Mr Leavitt: Correct, by looking at this stuff it could be correct.

Throughout the inquiry, Mr Leavitt told the commission he could not recall many events from 2021 and 2022.

It prompted the commissioner to ask if he had been diagnosed with any cognitive decline or had seen a medical practitioner about his apparent lack of recollection of events.

Mr Leavitt responded no.

He admitted he was a heavy drug user at the time and "in different hazy states".

The hearing continues tomorrow, when Mr Leavitt is expected to return to give more evidence.

title: Power player banned for six AFL matches for betting on games
text:
Port Adelaide footballer Josh Sinn has been suspended for six AFL matches for betting on league games, one of which involved his own club.

The AFL said Sinn placed bets totalling $195 on four matches, including one involving the Power.

But Sinn, who missed the season due to injury, did not play in the game.

The four bets were uncovered by an AFL Integrity Unit investigation and were placed between April 25 and May 2.

All were unsuccessful, according to the league, which said Sinn was "not found to have used any inside information in placing the bets".

Sinn has been banned from the opening six rounds of next year's AFL season, but will be allowed to play in practice and pre-season matches, as well as SANFL games that coincide with the AFL's rounds five and six.

Alcohol and gambling ads 'deeply embedded' in AFL Every NRL and AFL club has an alcohol sponsor this season while every NRL and five AFL clubs are sponsored by gambling companies, a new report has found.

The league said Sinn had admitted to the breach and apologised to both it and the Power.

AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said that, in determining the penalty, the league had "taken into account that [Sinn] did not play in any of the matches involved and was not found to have used inside information".

"Josh has admitted the conduct, accepted responsibility and expressed remorse," Harley said in a statement.

"Players know they cannot bet on AFL matches. Betting on a match involving your own club and teammates is particularly serious and, in this case, materially increased the sanction."

At a media conference this afternoon, Power CEO Matthew Richardson said the club was "extremely disappointed in Josh".

He said the club was first informed of the matter halfway through the year.

"We were first advised late in June, and that investigation was completed late last week," Richardson said.

"Josh is a young man who has made a very poor decision. Josh appreciates that, he's owning that.

"Our focus will be absolutely on supporting Josh as he now undertakes further education around gambling, and we'll support him in rebuilding his trust with our playing group, with our football club and with the community more broadly."

The league said Sinn would be required to undergo additional education to the gambling harm training that players received.

Richardson said the AFL had conducted a "really detailed investigation" into the breaches, which he described as "disappointing" and "stupid".

"What I do know is that the AFL have got really sophisticated tracking mechanisms," he said.

"The integrity of our game is paramount, but people make mistakes, and that's what's happened here. It's a serious mistake, hence the penalty."

title: Hundreds of tonnes of rubbish illegally dumped on WA roadsides each year
text:
Tonnes of rubbish and potentially toxic old building material are being dumped on Perth roadsides and nature strips by what is believed to be contractors and others avoiding council tip fees.

WA's Main Roads department says it has removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from the Perth metropolitan road network over the past two years.

Dianella resident Robert Parker told 102.5 ABC Perth he recently saw what appeared to be 10 tonnes of material by the side of Reid Highway when he was out walking.

"There's what appeared to be a bit of asbestos or fencing being dumped in the scrub down there," he said.

"Later on, I was driving and [it appeared] a commercial contractor has chosen to use the verge on Reid Highway as his yard and dumped asbestos material and other products that should go to landfill or the appropriate recycling facility."

Mr Parker said he reported the dumping to Main Roads, but also believed councils were making it too expensive for people to legally dispose of their hard rubbish.

"You go to the tips, and they say, 'Oh no, we don't accept super six fencing here anymore, we don't take hardy fence', or it's only so many sheets per time.

" And people just go and dump it in the bush. "

Construction waste dumped on the southern side of Reid Highway. (ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos)

Listeners to 102.5 ABC Radio Perth said there were significant barriers to disposing of rubbish legally.

Matt: 'It's very expensive to take waste to the recycling centre. Last week they would not accept some bathroom tiles. They said it was construction waste, and won't be accepted. No wonder people do illegal dumping.'

Anon: "It's a no-brainer: getting rid of waste in the community is far too expensive. It should be free and funded by the state government through our taxes, a clean city with proper disposal is good for everyone and everyone should pay through the taxes. Illegal dumping goes away then, and we return to a beautiful litter-free city."

Anon: "I took a broken office chair to the local tip. The guy on the gate said it would cost me $45 to dump it. I guess that's why people dump stuff illegally.'

Sivwarr: 'I drive up to Gidgegannup quite regularly on Toodyay road the illegal dumping starts at the bottom of the hills and just doesn't stop."

Others were less sympathetic

Rick: "The reason for illegal dumping is laziness, selfishness and a sense of self-entitlement."

Rubbish dumped on the southern side of Reid Highway between Camboon Road and Alexander Drive. (ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos)

In a statement, a Main Roads spokesperson said the department was aware of the fencing material on the southern side of Reid Highway.

"The material has been programmed for removal and will be cleared by a maintenance crew within the coming week," the spokesperson said.

"Across the 2024/25 and 2025/26 financial years, Main Roads removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from the metropolitan road network alone."

They said the department continued to monitor known dumping hotspots and used "targeted measures" to deter offending.

title: The longer-term thinking driving Swimming Australia's newest event
text:
Swim GP's Melbourne debut ticked plenty of boxes at the weekend.

A whole bevvy of happy swimmers and cheery coaches who were clearly fully invested in the contest, competing in front of packed stands, with plenty viewing at home too.

But Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse says this is only the start.

"Overall, [we're] really pleased," Woodhouse told ABC Sport, post the inaugural event.

"The two most pleasing aspects were the reaction and the buy-in from the athletes and coaches themselves … and the crowds.

Cheering fans were fully invested in the teams during the inaugural Swim GP. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"It's pretty rare that we can encourage and get young fans of swimming … getting them in the stands so they can watch the races and they can cheer and they can have their favourite team and favourite colours and things like that.

How Swim GP may have given a glimpse of the future of para-sport Swim GP's all-action, high-octane racing is designed to provide a boost for Australia's swimmers in the lead-up to LA28 and Brisbane 2032, and puts para-swimming front and centre.

"The reaction in the actual venue of the crowd, and a really good young crowd, was terrific. That's what we're aiming to do."

More than 3,500 supporters enjoyed the inaugural event live at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre in Albert Park, with Saturday night's session a complete sellout.

The made-for-TV event was also a boost for Channel Nine, who helped to develop the event, with Swimming Australia saying it achieved a peak reach of 1.13 million people, and an average audience of 237,000 for Friday night's offering.

In the currency of the modern media landscape, almost 3 million social media views sealed the deal for what was a productive evening all round.

It certainly went some way to help cement the current crop of Dolphins as celebrities in their own right, ahead of a huge six years of sport that culminates with the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

A ready-made fan base

The fans embraced the swimmers in Melbourne. ( Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swimming Australia made no secret of its aim to targeting a younger age group, between five and 15 years of age, to build its athletes' brand — and it has a ready-made fan base that already exists in plain sight.

Three of the four teams: Kingtide, Wahoo and Kraken were partnered with swim-school providers Carlile, Rackley and GoSwim/Belgravia respectively, who have around 200 learn-to-swim schools around the country.

Woodhouse confirmed that integrating the estimated 600,000 families and 1 million kids who are involved in learn-to-swim programs with the Dolphins was a key part of the organisation's wider strategy leading into Brisbane 2032.

Swimming Australia wants its learn-to-swim participants to learn to love the sport. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"The wider message is about the industry and us and our athletes, Paralympic and Olympic athletes, engaging all the way down to learn-to-swim level," Woodhouse explained.

"If you get kids picking up a ball at four or five years of age then they're probably going to get hooked and join [a football team].

"In swimming we should be in the retention game, not the recruitment game.

"These providers like Rackley and Carlisle and Belgravia, getting them involved with this event they'll start, through those respective teams, to build a far greater awareness of Swim GP, of the teams and of the athletes, which brings in the younger fans.

"If we can build all of that fandom in the lead up to Brisbane '32, then we're going to be in a lot better position in five or six years."

Swim GP shone a spotlight on Australia's Dolphins. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Then there's the question of keeping athletes in the sport for as long as possible to spread important water safety messages.

"Certainly we have a long-term vision of Swimming Australia to be able to have athletes on contract where we're able to pay them to be ambassadors for, not just for the sport and swimming for Australia at Paralympics and at Olympics, but to actually be the custodians of those really important messages of drowning prevention and swimming safe," Woodhouse said.

"If we start doing that and keep kids in the sport longer, not about racing or anything like that, but just that fun element, then we're going to get the natural flow of all kids joining clubs and then going potentially into that pathway of competitive swimming and building up into higher performance pathways.

"It's a big flow-on effect, but it's a system-wide integration … being able to engage with everyone in the industry for the benefit of everyone, particularly for the kids."

Learnings from the ISL and ahead to LA28

Swimming Australia wants its swimmers exposed to big crowds in the lead up to LA. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP is not a new concept, with Woodhouse leaning on his experiences with the International Swimming League (ISL), where he was chief executive of the London Roar franchise.

Woodhouse said there were discussions to get an Australia-based franchise into the league before it ran into a litany of problems, headlined by COVID.

That was enough to suggest Australia was ready for its own version of the competition, that and the prospect that Australia will become the centre of the swimming world in the coming years.

"I'm very confident, and our team are very confident, that Australia will become the centralised location for elite swimming between 2028 and 2032," Woodhouse said.

"Just as we want our athletes to go and get experience in California and race in LA, as they've done this year and last year ahead of the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, a lot of the other athletes from around the world are going to want to come to Australia to compete, to acclimatise, to train and things like that.

Australia is primed to be the centre of the swimming world in the coming years. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"So we've got two or three years to build the models from Swim GP, but I actually believe we've got enough talent and big names here in Australia to build it without any international athletes.

"Then, if internationals do want to come after the '28 Olympics and Paralympics and compete with us, then obviously they'd be welcomed.

"But we've got a strong enough base of athletes here to make it a big success."

Part of that involves moving the competition around to different cities, perhaps by having a series of two or three meetings take place around the country.

And although this was "pressure-free" competition, with no emphasis on times of making squads, there is also a high performance element at play.

Although Swim GP was fun, coaches want to up the pressure. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"Both our head coaches, [Paralympic head coach] Mel Tantrum and [Olympic head coach] Rowan Taylor [said] they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials," Woodhouse said.

"The [LA28] Olympic team, they're competing at SoFi Stadium, 40,000 screaming Americans, while the Paralympic team will be down at Long Beach with 4,000 or 5,000 fans.

"Particularly for the Para-athletes, some of those athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"[The crowd in LA] will make a hell of a lot of noise and it's very intimidating," Woodhouse, who has experience to lean on as a bronze medallist in the 400m IM at the last LA Games in 1984, continued.

"There are different pressures, of course; this was all about fun and entertainment. But there are those really important experiential benefits for them as well."

title: Pacific country to propose three-child limit to slow surging population
text:
Lorna Iseu always wanted a big family.

As a mother of five, she got her wish, but she wouldn't necessarily encourage others to do the same.

"I've now realised having a big family isn't cheap," she said.

"I'd encourage couples to have at least two or three children. For me, five is quite stressful."

Lorna Iseu lives in Port Moresby with her husband and five children. (ABC News: Belinda Kora)

Papua New Guinea's prime minister, James Marape, may well agree.

His government has announced plans to introduce a new national family planning policy to curb the country's high birth rate.

Under the proposed policy outlined in a press release, families would be encouraged to have no more than three children, in a move that draws comparisons with China's now-abandoned one-child policy, which remained in place until 2015.

While still at the proposal stage, PNG's policy aims to prevent unplanned pregnancies, ease pressure on government services and household budgets, and slow the country's population growth.

James Marape has proposed a new national family planning policy. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Official statistics put PNG's population at about 10.18 million, and it's growing by more than 180,000 people annually.

But economists question the reliability of the country's census data, suggesting the actual population could be closer to 12 million.

Teenage pregnancies and high rural birth rates are among the factors believed to be contributing to the country's population surge.

Health experts also say limited access to health care and contraception is forcing many women to have more children than they would otherwise choose to have.

Official statistics put Papua New Guinea's population at about 10.18 million. (Reuters)

Hidden figures

Ms Iseu lives in the country's capital, Port Moresby.

Her husband works as a security guard, while she stays home to look after her three youngest children.

Her two eldest attend school.

"My children can't even sit properly in the classroom. Some sit on desks, many are on the floor; it's so overcrowded," she said.

Margaret Ropa, also a mother of five from Port Moresby, agrees, saying the sheer number of children in the public school system has forced her to send her children to private school.

"You have 85 kids in a classroom," she said.

A 2025 national reform road map, titled Reset@50, which outlines the government's priorities for the next 20 years, notes PNG's fertility rate at 3.6 children per woman.

The document reports an adolescent birth rate of 64.9 births per 1,000 girls and women aged 15 to 19, well above the global average of about 38 per 1,000, according to World Bank data.

Meanwhile, only 25 per cent of women of reproductive age used modern contraceptive methods.

Margaret Ropa says the sheer number of children in the public school system forces many families to send their children to private schools. (Supplied)

A fertility rate of 3.6 in a country of 10 million equates to roughly 250,000 to 300,000 births a year.

Kingtau Mambon, an economics lecturer at the University of Papua New Guinea, told the ABC that PNG's annual number of births was likely at the top end of that range.

"I've talked to doctors, and they say the birth rate is around 300,000 per year," he said.

Medical experts say PNG has a fertility rate of 3.6 children per woman. (ABC News: Marian Faa)

Mr Mambon believes the National Statistical Office's population figure of 10.18 million is likely low, saying the real figure could be as high as 12 million.

He said the most recent census, in 2024, may not be fully accurate because it included only six questions and was affected by logistical and administrative breakdowns.

He said he had to go looking for census officers to take the survey.

"I was actually running after the people who brought the questionnaires," he said.

"They should have been looking for me."

The ABC contacted the PNG government for comment on the country's population, the census and the proposed policy.

PNG's 2024 census included only six questions and was marred by logistical and administrative breakdowns. (ABC News: Marian Faa)

Mr Mambon said he spoke to many people in central Port Moresby who did not complete the census, and he believed the same was true in rural areas, where he sees most of the population growth occurring.

He said customs around land ownership were one reason families were so large.

"The thing with PNG is, men own the land, and to defend the land you need a lot of people," he said.

"So men have to pursue the interests of protecting the land and tribal heritage.

"They have to have more kids."

Mr Mambon said stigma around contraception in rural areas was also pushing fertility rates higher.

Grassroots births and deaths register could help uncover PNG's population A Papua New Guinean researcher calls for Australia to help deliver its next national census amid speculation the population is as high as 17 million.

"Many of the health facilities are being run by NGOs of faith-based organisations," he said.

"From the faith-based point of view, some don't want to give out contraceptives."

A holistic approach

Ms Ropa said she believed the government was doing the right thing with its policy proposal, but was sceptical about how it would be taken up, particularly in villages and rural areas.

Anjelique Giranah, country director of Marie Stopes PNG, an NGO providing family planning and reproductive health services, said encouraging people to have fewer children wouldn't work unless the government empowered women to have a bigger say in family sizes.

Kingtau Mambon says he believes the country's population could be as high as 12 million. (ABC News: Natalie Whiting )

She said limited access to health care and contraception, as well as expectations from family and spouses, meant women were having more children than they wanted.

"National research confirms many women who want to delay or avoid having children are not able to access the contraception they need," she said.

"For us, meaningful choice means a woman can access reliable information and a range of contraceptive options and at the same time make that voluntary decision without pressure or coercion."

title: Melbourne Cup runner So You Are found in Sydney skip bin
text:
Melbourne Cup runner So You Are has been found in a Sydney skip, one day after it died from a severe bout of colic.

Sydney man Gregg Jowett released a video on social media after he discovered a horse in a skip at Lucas Heights that appeared to share the markings of So You Are, which finished eighth in this year's Melbourne Cup.

REC Equine Specialists confirmed the horse in Mr Jowett's video was So You Are.

Trainer Bjorn Baker said he expected a full explanation from REC Equine Specialists about how and why the horse's remains ended up in a skip bin.

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said.

"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserves to be treated with respect and dignity after his death.

"I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.

"My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family [owners], and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss."

Video of So You Are in a skip bin, filmed by Sydney resident Gregg Jowett, has rocked the racing industry. (Facebook: Gregg Jowett)

REC Equine Specialists released a statement extending its deepest sympathy to the owners, trainer, and connections of So You Are, unreservedly apologising for the distress the video caused.

"After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," it said.

"What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone else who cared for him. We are deeply sorry."

REC said it was not responsible for the burial of So You Are, but said it should have known how the horse was handled after leaving its care.

"So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that," it said.

"We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.

"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally. We are working with our service provider and the facility operators, together with Racing NSW, to establish how this happened and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again."

So You Are died from colic 13 days after running in the 2026 Melbourne Cup. (Getty Images: Racing Photos/George Sal)

So You Are had a successful spring, winning four times including a trio of Group 3 races at Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.

The five-year-old finished eighth in the Melbourne Cup, won by Point Of Law.

REC said it would no longer use the service provider and was reviewing how service providers it contracted cared for horses after death, from collection to final burial.

It said it would share the findings with Racing NSW.

Waste management company Cleanaway, which runs the Lucas Heights landfill, said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area of the site.

"Cleanaway's Lucas Heights landfill is licensed to accept and dispose of animal carcasses," a spokesperson said.

"The horse carcass delivered to the facility arrived in a small tipper truck, which is not permitted on the landfill tipping face for safety reasons.

"In accordance with established procedures, the carcass was transferred into a skip bin to enable its safe disposal at the landfill."

'Distressing and completely unacceptable'

The fallout from the distressing footage of deceased Melbourne Cup runner So You Are in a skip bin has been immediate.

ABC Sport understands that interim Racing NSW boss Graeme Hinton is working to create new industry standards to ensure animals are provided with dignity and respect after their death.

It is understood the new standards will be released at the end of the month.

Racehorse So You Are dies of colic Trainer Bjorn Baker says the five-year-old horse, which finished eighth in the Melbourne Cup, was rushed to hospital but died following a severe bout of colic.

Racing NSW released a statement saying So You Are was awaiting burial when the video was recorded, and that it would conduct an investigation.

"The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect," the statement said.

"Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner.

"If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action."

Animal Justice Party NSW Upper House MP Emma Hurst held a press conference in Sydney following the treatment of So You Are.

She said the news was "absolutely heartbreaking", but not surprising.

"This horse has been treated as though he is nothing more than a piece of rubbish," she said.

"To be completely honest, I'm not entirely surprised. We've had complaints about the racing industry for the entire eight years that I have been in parliament," she said.

"There are serious questions around the entire racing industry, and this most recent incident just raises more questions."

She called for greater transparency and accountability within the racing industry and called on the state government for further action.

title: Family of veteran who died after 18-hour ambulance wait call for answers
text:
The family of a 20-year Navy veteran who died after waiting more than 18 hours for a Queensland ambulance is demanding answers.

The Thornlands man's family said his wife first called Triple Zero (000) on Friday afternoon and made further calls that went unattended.

"When she called on Saturday morning to say he was no longer breathing, paramedics arrived at the door within six minutes," the family said in a statement.

The man has been described by his family as a much-loved husband, father and grandfather.

"He served his country in the Royal Australian Navy for 20 years. He dedicated a significant part of his life to serving Australia," the family said.

"When he needed help himself, it did not come.

"His wife is now left asking herself what more she could have done. Nobody who called for help that many times should be left with that question."

The man in his 70s is one of three Queenslanders who have died in recent days while waiting for an ambulance.

His family said they did not know whether he could have been saved and would wait on the coroner to provide answers.

"What we do know is that, had he been taken to hospital, he would at least have had the opportunity to receive medical care," the family said in a statement.

"And if nothing could have been done, we would have had the chance to be by his side and say goodbye. That opportunity was taken from us"

His family has called for accountability and meaningful changes to ensure no other family endures the grief they are experiencing.

'Avoidable deaths'

Also on Saturday, a Logan man in his 50s died after waiting for five and a half hours for an ambulance.

On Monday, a man in Brisbane's south in his 80s died after waiting almost four hours for paramedics.

And a man also in his 80s died earlier this month waiting for an ambulance in Townsville, with the local hospital's emergency department capacity at 107 per cent at that time.

Health minister Tim Nicholls told parliament he had been briefed on the preventable deaths of three people who were waiting for an ambulance.

Health Minister Tim Nicholls was briefed on the three preventable deaths over the weekend. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"Any avoidable death is one too many, and I can confirm that all of those avoidable deaths are currently being investigated by the Queensland Ambulance Service and Clinical Incident Review Teams," he said.

"I want to pass on my condolences to all of the family and the loved ones of those who passed."

Mr Nicholls said he had sought assurance from the Queensland Ambulance Service (QAS) and the Queensland Ambulance Commissioner that the families have been contacted.

Delays 'unacceptable'

There were almost 13,000 Triple Zero calls over the last weekend, with over 70 per cent of those requiring immediate assistance.

A QAS spokesperson said the death of any patient was a tragedy, and it was supporting those affected.

"It is unacceptable that patients requiring urgent care experience delays, which is why we are doing as much as we can to respond to incidents in a timely manner," they said.

"We are working closely with hospitals to support the timely transfer of patients to emergency departments so paramedics can return to the community and respond to patients requiring urgent care."

Australian Medical Association Queensland President Associate Professor Erica Gannon says emergency workers are "only human". (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Australian Medical Association Queensland President Erica Gannon, said the incidents were concerning and showed the pressure clinicians were under.

"Our wonderful ambulance officers, our doctors and our nurses are working through their capacity, but they're only human. They can only work with the resources that we have," Associate Professor Gannon said.

"We can't off-ramp people in our emergency departments and free up our emergency crews to go and treat more patients in our community if we can't offload them."

title: What to know about the online banking delays affecting major US banks
text:
A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase has caused problems throughout the United States financial system.

Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major banks and the money transfer service Zelle in relation to the issue on Monday.

Here's what we know.

What's behind the outage?

JPMorgan Chase, the largest US bank by total assets, said a software bug was affecting its internal hardware systems and causing transaction delays.

The company was working to bring banking services back online.

Some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later."

JPMorgan Chase, the largest US bank by total assets, says it has been affected by a software bug. (AP Photo: LM Otero)

Were other banks affected?

In a sense, yes.

Customers at Bank of America, Citigroup and other banks trying to transact with Chase may have seen their transactions slow, even though those banks were not having issues with their services.

"Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," explained Joe Evangelisti, a spokesperson for Chase.

What about Zelle?

Zelle was not directly affected by the Chase glitch.

But customers at other banks may have experienced transaction delays while trying to send or receive Zelle payments involving a Chase customer.

Zelle is a rapid peer-to-peer payment system used by major US banks.

The platform is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.

A spokesperson for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.

Was this a cyber attack?

Chase said that the technical problem was not the result of a cyber attack, stressing that it was an isolated incident and not related to anything other than a bug.

When might service be fully restored?

Chase said its customers still had access to their accounts and funds.

The company expects the issue to be resolved by the end of day Monday.

Was this related to the Microsoft and air traffic disruptions last week?

No. While the disruptions took place just days apart, government officials and company leaders have said they were unrelated.

Outage to cost 'billions' Some small businesses have lost up to $30,000 in one day.

The major outage by Microsoft on Thursday that lasted for hours, severely impacting services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, was due to a technical issue that arose during an upgrade.

The tech giant has said there is "no indication" that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, such as a cyber attack, or action by artificial intelligence agents.

Another outage that affected the nation's air traffic control system Friday, grounding all US flights for several hours and disrupting domestic air travel over the weekend, was caused by a router that malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system.

AP

title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback despite backing from big names
text:
Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating the scandal-hit Jensen Huang as chief executive, three people have told Reuters.

Mr Huang was forced to step down last week amid revelations about affairs involving employees and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

The former chief executive's departure plunged the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sent shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll.

More than 180,200 people, including thousands identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, have signed a petition demanding Mr Huang's return.

Elon Musk has also thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump, who reportedly held millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, said he would not mind seeing Mr Huang reinstated as CEO.

Mr Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $US13 million ($19m) and $US62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, The Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures.

Campaign gaining traction

Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen".

The message "Taiwan heart Jensen" was projected on the Taipei 101 building in Taipei in support of Jensen Huang. (Reuters: Ann Wang)

It came as the Stand With Jensen campaign gained traction online.

"We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," an open letter published on the campaign's website said.

The campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories.

Prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace Mr Huang before all the facts are known.

However, a person familiar with the matter said: "The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back."

Large investors are risk-averse

The uncertainty over Mr Huang's future has divided investors and complicated the board's search for a successor.

Nvidia has lost $US800 billion in market value since Mr Huang stepped down.

Who is Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang? After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why?

The company's shares closed down more than 4 per cent on Monday, a day before the chipmaker was due to report third-quarter earnings.

Independent technology researcher Richard Windsor said he expected "very risk-averse" large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Mr Huang's return while investigations remained unresolved, because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create.

At the centre of the scandal is Chinese businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang (no relation), who Mr Huang admitted to having an affair with.

US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, sources said.

Huang's exit rocks Taiwan

Mr Huang's reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed "Jensanity".

Nvidia relies on a local manufacturer to make its most advanced chips, and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture other chips and systems underpinning the AI boom.

For many Taiwanese, Mr Huang's exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global AI boom.

Jimmy Yang, a 42-year-old marketing worker, said Mr Huang's departure was a loss for Taiwan.

He expressed hope that Mr Huang could eventually return to Nvidia.

"His private life is his own choice," Mr Yang said.

"But whether it's the night market economy he's driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive," he said.

Reuters/ABC

title: Melbourne council apologises to Macedonian community over Moomba flag ban
text:
The City of Melbourne has apologised to members of the Australian Macedonian community after it prohibited a culturally significant flag from being displayed at this year's Moomba Parade.

The Star of Kutlesh, also known as the Vergina Sun and Kutlesh Sun, is associated with Alexander the Great and has been part of a longstanding dispute between Greece and the Republic of North Macedonia.

While the image is a protected national symbol of Greece, others argue the flag represents the wider Macedonian ethnicity, which transcends the modern national boundaries of Greece, North Macedonia, and Bulgaria.

Earlier this year, the Federation of Macedonian Cultural Artistic Associations (FOMKUD) withdrew its Moomba performance after Melbourne City Council announced the flag could not be shown due to a ban on symbols that may be politically divisive.

Today the council's head of business, economy and activation wrote to the community stating it could fly the flag at future events, after an independent review found banning the flag had a "significant and unintended negative impact".

"Our decision left many performers, families and community leaders feeling their cultural identity and heritage were not respected or properly understood," the letter from Sara Quon stated.

"I sincerely apologise."

The flag was allowed to be shown at the 2019 Moomba parade. (Supplied: MKUD Jane Sandanski Macedonian Cultural and Artistic Association)

FOMKUD secretary Stoj Jovevski said the community was relieved, saying the flag did not serve any political purpose.

"Everyone's excited," he said.

"It unites all Macedonian people under the one flag, under the one language, under the one culture and tradition," he said.

But the Pan-Macedonian Association of Melbourne and Victoria, which supported the initial ban, accused the council of not consulting its community.

"It's pretty much taking away our own identity," the organisation's president Peter Stefanidis said.

"We are very upset we weren't consulted at all."

Apology a win for minority group, federation says

The Star of Kutlesh flag, which depicts a yellow sun on a red background, incorporates a symbol found at a tomb believed to contain the remains of Alexander the Great's father.

Those with ties to Greece and North Macedonia claim the image as integral to their cultural history.

Following the fall of Yugoslavia in 1991, the Republic of Macedonia declared its independence and adopted the Kutlesh Sun as its national flag, which ignited a bitter dispute with neighbouring Greece.

In 1995, the Republic of Macedonia changed its flag, and three-years later agreed to change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia and prohibit the public use of the image.

"North Macedonia has agreed that it's a Greek symbol," Mr Stefanidis said.

Earlier this year, Melbourne council wrote to FOMKUD stating a "high level of sensitivity around flags" meant any "cultural or regional" flags would not be allowed at Moomba, adding only "national and organisational flags" were permitted.

This prompted a group of 80 dancers to withdraw their Moomba performance.

A subsequent independent review found council "staff acted in good faith with community safety in mind," but ultimately conceded the decision felt short of community expectations.

It invited the dance group to participate in next year's event, "including the display of the Star of Kutlesh flag".

A statement from the City of Melbourne said: "We recognise the hurt caused to the Macedonian community by restricting a flag of deep cultural significance."

Melbourne City Council has invited the federation's performers to take part in next year's Moomba parade. (ABC News: Natasha Schapova)

Mr Jovevski, the secretary of FOMKUD, said the initial decision left many in his community shocked

"Whether you come from northern Greece or Republic of [North] Macedonia or Western Bulgaria, if you feel Macedonian in your heart … nobody should be able to stop it," he said.

He added council's decision was a "win" for other minority groups.

"There are a lot of minority groups that experience our plight," he said.

"So, part of the win is for those people those other minority groups that are getting bullied, and their cultural expression suppressed."

FOMKUD said it would participate in next year's event.

title: Greens offer government a path to pass trusts and capital gains tax changes
text:
The Greens could pass Labor's two major tax bills by the end of next week if the minor party can extract a promise to reform the charities sector.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers wants parliament's support for legislation to impose a minimum tax on some trusts and to carve out start-ups from the new capital gains tax (CGT) regime.

The Coalition is opposed, making the Greens the only viable pathway in the Senate.

The minor party is comfortable with the principle of both measures and would support them subject to a small number of changes, several Greens sources told the ABC.

The party's red line is an exemption for private schools and other non-tax-paying recipients, which they want repealed along with a commitment to consider broader charitable sector reform, including the tax treatment of religious institutions.

But the Greens have no apparent red lines on the CGT start-up carve-out and appear unlikely to support independent MP Allegra Spender's proposed alternative, despite expressing openness to it yesterday.

Mr Chalmers revealed this morning that he had written to Ms Spender outlining Treasury's concerns with her proposal.

That letter, seen by the ABC, said her idea would be "neither simple nor straightforward" and would be inequitable.

Spender proposal not 'fairer', Chalmers says

The CGT issue relates to a workaround the government devised in response to a complaint from start-ups that the new inflation-based discount would unfairly penalise them, because they start from scratch and so had no cost base to be "inflated".

The government's proposed concession would apply to businesses less than 15 years old, subject to a test to establish whether they were developing or commercialising "genuinely innovative products, processes, services or methods".

Government won't promise net savings Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update.

Ms Spender said the exemption was too narrow and subjective and that any "active" business assets should instead get a 40 per cent discount, which she said would raise a similar amount of money but be simpler.

In his letter to Ms Spender, Mr Chalmers said Treasury had "identified a number of issues and concerns".

"Their analysis suggests that your proposal is unlikely to be simpler, fairer or enhance productivity, as you suggest," he wrote.

"Your proposal would introduce a second set of tax arrangements for capital gains and replaces one arbitrary distortion in the tax system with another, for the majority of assets. [It] risks introducing more complexity, not less."

In the letter, Mr Chalmers said early-stage start-ups, which were most likely to be innovative, would likely stand to pay higher taxes under the 40 per cent idea and that identifying which assets were "active" would be complex.

"This would need to occur regularly and across all businesses to ensure shareholders understand an entity's status, as opposed to the current definition that only applies to small businesses in years where CGT events arise," he wrote.

He added that the proposal could "introduce pervasive incentives to restructure for tax reasons", such as by putting properties and other assets into an "active" business vehicle to pay less tax.

Call to listen to business

In a statement, Ms Spender told the ABC her proposal was "gathering wide support in the business community" and reiterated her call to the government to "listen seriously to what business is saying and carefully analyse and evaluate the advantages" of her model.

"I would welcome a thorough and serious parliamentary inquiry," she said.

Ms Spender added that she "appreciated" the letter but that it had "failed to recognise the concerns of the business community" with the existing approach "and its real-world impacts on risk-taking and investment...

"The business community wasn't consulted on the government's original CGT direction but is willing to compromise. The government should be willing to listen now."

Loading...

Greens sources told the ABC the party had no particular inclination to support Ms Spender's proposal, saying that Senator McKim's suggestion yesterday that he was "open" to it should not be read as an endorsement.

The sources said the minor party was broadly supportive of the idea of giving innovative start-ups the option to choose between the old 50 per cent discount and the new discount.

The Greens opted not to support a Coalition motion today to refer the bill, which also includes research and development tax incentive changes and changes to the EV discount, to a Senate inquiry reporting in the new year.

But the minor party is keeping its options open on that front and sees no urgency to pass either of the tax bills by the end of the year if the government is unwilling to give ground.

Charitable exemption for trusts under microscope

On trusts, the Greens' sole concern is that an exemption for charitable giving is too broad, allowing people to escape the 30 per cent tax not just by giving to registered charities but to any income tax-exempt entity, including private schools and sporting clubs.

Greens decry private school trust loophole Treasurer Jim Chalmers is preparing to introduce legislation for a 30 per cent tax on discretionary trusts on Wednesday amid fierce business opposition.

Senator McKim, the party's economic spokesperson, used a Senate inquiry into the bill to recommend this be restricted to registered charities only, and that the government agree to respond to a 2024 Productivity Commission report into charity rules.

That report found the granting of "deductible gift recipient" and tax-exempt status to non-charities had "no coherent policy rationale". It advocated excluding private and religious schools and religious activities.

A Greens source emphasised that the government would not necessarily need to agree to go this far, but that there was appetite to see the issue probed.

Recent scrutiny over the election activity of Exclusive Brethren church members was cited as a motivator.

The source said another recommendation from the inquiry, to facilitate a public register of trusts and their beneficiaries, was not a red line for negotiations.

No rush to pass by end of year

Sources said there had been no tangible progress to report on any concessions.

When the Greens' concerns about private schools were first reported by the ABC last month, Mr Chalmers said he had learned of the concern from the reporting.

"I haven't had the opportunity to engage directly … we've tried to make sure that there are reasonable arrangements for charities, for not-for-profits, which reflect some of the current arrangements that are in place," he told Radio National at the time.

"There are good reasons for those sorts of exemptions. [Private school giving] is a very specific sliver of what's being proposed here."

title: Bunnings cuts 230 jobs in partial offshoring of tech services
text:
Hardware retailer Bunnings will cut roughly 230 jobs and end 120 contractor agreements as it shifts part of its technology department offshore.

The Australian retail giant announced today it had penned a new agreement with Indian-based tech firm Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) as part of a restructure of its technology services.

Roughly 230 permanent roles will be made redundant and an additional 120 contractor roles will end as a result.

Australia cashes in on India's IT jobs machine India has positioned itself as a global hub of skilled, cheap labour, and Australian companies are moving more jobs to its shores.

In a statement, Bunnings managing director Mike Schneider said the changes aimed to respond to evolving consumer needs.

"This is a necessary but important change. We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us," Mr Schneider said.

The transition is due to begin in December and continue through to June next year, the company said.

Affected staff will be supported in their roles over Christmas, with job losses to begin in the new year, while the retailer will retain a core in-house technology team of approximately 500 people based in Australia. Remaining services will be delivered by TCS teams based in Australia, India and the Philippines.

Mike Schneider says impacted staff are being offered support. (Supplied: Bunnings)

Mr Schneider said Bunnings would support impacted team members through various means, including redundancy packages.

"We know that this is difficult for our Technology team members, particularly those impacted by the change," he said.

"We're managing these changes with care and respect, including through redundancy packages, career transition, redeployment wherever possible and wellbeing support."

Bunnings is the latest in a growing list of Australian companies, including Qantas, NAB, Officeworks, Woolworths and Coles, to announce plans to outsource jobs overseas.

'Difficult news to share', executive says

Staff were given the news earlier today by Bunnings chief information officer Genevie Elliott, who said it was "difficult news to share".

In a virtual meeting with employees, Ms Elliott said many of those impacted by today's announcement had helped build up the company's technology services, which remained in use across its network of stores.

Bunnings is the latest major Australian company to offshore part of its operation. (ABC News: Madigan Landry )

"I want you to know these changes we're announcing are not a reflection of anyone's performance or their contribution or value," she told staff.

"So I think it's really important you all understand why we've made this decision. Over the last two years, we've deliberately strengthened our tech function.

"We've evolved our structure, our ways of working, how we prioritise and deliver work, and that structure has served us well.

"I don't want anyone thinking those changes didn't work. They did. But this decision that I'm sharing today builds on that work."

Ms Elliott said bringing TCS on board would allow the company to drive down business costs and tap into "specialist expertise and global retail experience".

"We need a model that allows us to remain competitive without continually increasing our costs. This partnership will help us do that," she said.

She said the company had to evolve alongside a rapidly transforming online retail environment impacting how consumers shop.

"And we all know that tech is rapidly evolving, and the pace of change is only going to increase. That means we need to respond to keep up."

title: New live-stream cameras at Canberra Hospital's baby intensive care unit
text:
For New South Wales mother Erin Thorpe, the birth of her daughter Aubree has been a "journey".

Aubree, Ms Thorpe's sixth child, was born prematurely at 30 weeks and five days' gestation, and has spent her first weeks out in the world at the Canberra Hospital.

Before the arrival of new 24-hour live-streaming cameras at the hospital, it had been 9 and a half weeks since Ms Thorpe had been home to Goulburn.

Ms Thorpe said the cameras had brought "extra reassurance" while caring for her other children.

"They've come down to Canberra on weekends and we've gone out and about, and I’ve just got this feeling that, 'I’ve got to be back at the hospital now, let's go'," Ms Thorpe said.

" Since the cameras have been rolling, I just log on, and I can see that she's fine. "

The system places a camera at each cot, with parents able to opt in or out. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

The AngelEyes cameras have been installed at the hospital's Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) and Special Care Nursery (SCN), allowing parents to see their babies at any time of day.

Ms Thorpe said it meant the rest of her family, including Aubree's five siblings, could connect with her over the course of her hospital stay, and follow her progress.

"Seeing how they look at her, and they're kind of making those connections with her that they can't make," Ms Thorpe said.

" When they first met her, they used to call the CPAP machine the 'snorkel', and [now] they're like, 'she doesn't have the snorkel anymore!', which is exciting. "

Baby Aubree was born prematurely and has been in the neonatal unit in Canberra. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

A 'significant upgrade'

Baby cameras have previously been used in the Canberra Hospital's Special Care Nursery, after being first introduced in 2009.

But the cameras have never been used in the NICU, and the new system is a "significant upgrade", according to the Canberra Health Service's Clinical Lead, Hazel Carlisle.

Dr Hazel Carlisle says the cameras make it easier for interstate families to connect. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

"It can work in the dark or at times of low light, so we can protect babies' eyes from lots of light, and it's mobile, so it can be moved to fit the baby. So if the baby moves slightly, we can move the camera," Dr Carlisle said.

She said bedside contact was encouraged, but the cameras expanded options for families.

"The technology really helps to support families; it helps them to be reassured that their baby is safe and looked after," she said.

Dr Carlisle said the system was part of a family integrated care model, implemented after feedback from families.

Now, the NICU and SCN's combined 39 cots each have a movable camera, purchased through a $117,600 donation from the Newborn Intensive Care Foundation.

ACT Health Minister Marisa Paterson said privacy was "paramount", with each family given a unique secure login.

"There are all sorts of safeguards and monitoring and assurance arrangements in place to maintain the integrity of the system," she said.

"It's just an exciting step forward; it's allowing technology to be able to provide this incredibly important service for families."

title: Wallabies in danger of missing 'big three' target
text:
Coach Les Kiss is determined to ensure Australia finishes among the top three Southern Hemisphere teams in the Nations Championship after a rare weekend blowout for the Wallabies, All Blacks and Springboks.

For only the second time in rugby history, all of the "big three" were turned over on the same weekend by Northern Hemisphere opposition as South Africa lost 21-19 in France, New Zealand were sensationally beaten 35-28 in Wales and Australia lost narrowly 15-12 to Scotland at Murrayfield.

That had only previously occurred in July 2022, when all three suffered home defeats: New Zealand losing 23-12 to Ireland in Dunedin, South Africa going down 13-12 to Wales in Bloemfontein and Australia falling 25-17 to England in Brisbane.

Now, Australia has fallen to fourth in the Southern Hemisphere table of the Nations Championship, leapfrogged by Argentina, and should the Wallabies succumb to a fifth-straight Test defeat against Wales on Saturday, it will finish in that position.

Should Argentina upset France, even a Wallabies win would not be enough to claw them back to that third spot.

Wallabies attacking woes The Wallabies once again show precious little in an attacking sense, as Scotland edge a "turgid" encounter at Murrayfield.

But Kiss made it clear this would represent failure for a team that had come on its British sojourn seeking a top-three finish.

"We were aiming for the top-three when we came here, New Zealand and South Africa already being up there and going to be hard to reel in," Kiss said.

"So we were aiming for the top-three for sure, and that's what we'll measure ourselves on."

It is still only halfway through the tour, but the grim scenario of a second-straight European wipe-out looms following defeats in England, Italy, Ireland and France last year, the first time in 67 years that such a whitewash had occurred.

Les Kiss has watched his Wallabies side lose four Tests on the trot. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

Asked if the Wallabies had lost their confidence, Kiss mused: "Yeah, you do want a team with a bit of swagger. There's been losses throughout the last few years that have seemed to hang on, that's for sure.

"I wouldn't say it's confidence, I wouldn't say it's just belief. I think it's a mixture of those things coming together and it's just down to them believing that they can now win those big moments."

He referred to that last-second burst down the right touchline on Sunday, when Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen and Tom Wright could not quite turn the break into a match-winning moment.

"The losses obviously takes its toll but, mate, they're hardy and they're going to continue to work hard," Kiss said.

It all gives Saturday's Test against a Welsh side currently residing on cloud nine even more of a "must-win" feel.

Wales beat All Blacks Wales has pulled off one of the greatest wins in its recent history, beating the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years in a Nations Championship boilover.

Captain Harry Wilson counters: "Every Test match is must-win. We're going to go into the Wales game with the same attitude we do every time. We need a win. We're going to do everything in our power to make sure we can."

But Kiss admitted the incredible Welsh win over the All Blacks, their first in 73 years, had "changed everyone's minds" about Steve Tandy's reinvented team.

"Honestly, it was compelling. It was phenomenal what they did. So we're going to need to be good to go there on a short turnaround."

But could Australia be facing a side with energy levels zapped from their legs after throwing themselves into a record-breaking 346 tackles against New Zealand? Kiss just smiled: "Nah, they'll be energised. That's inspiring what they did, isn't it?

"We've just got to make sure we've got our reason to be up for it too, which is that it's a bloody important Test match to win."

AAP

title: Big Build royal commission as it happened: Bikie Joel Leavitt blames past ‘drug habit’ for false timesheets while working as CFMEU safety rep
text:
Thanks for following our live coverage of the sixth day of public hearings for the Big Build royal commission.

We heard from just one witness today – Joel Leavitt, a bikie and former CFMEU health and safety official whose job on a Big Build project made headlines when The Age first broke the Building Bad series back in July 2024.

When Cameron Bancroft made his first Sheffield Shield century in a year against South Australia at Adelaide Oval two weeks ago, the celebration was meaningful. After cutting a boundary, he sank to his knees with what looked like relief. And not just relief – it was noticeable that a weight appeared to be lifted from his shoulders. Cameron Bancroft. Getty Images The weight had not just been about making hundreds. Australia’s return to South Africa for a first Test series since 2018 had sat very heavily on Bancroft’s shoulders, given that there was always a chance his name would be dragged back into it as the player who used sandpaper on the ball. But ahead of that innings, Bancroft had told those close to him he was informed that Usman Khawaja intended to come forward with his recollections of the Sandpapergate episode, a version of events that showed in detail why there was a case for collective responsibility from the team.

Advertisement

Following a bruising couple of weeks for Australian cricket, Bancroft now has the opportunity to open up with an account that can be more complete than anything yet aired. Though David Warner and Steve Smith both served longer bans, no player was affected more greatly by the scandal than Bancroft. While it is true he briefly returned to the Test team in 2019, the majority of the past eight years have seen him unable to make the kind of mark on the game that would have helped balance what remains a hugely problematic period in the team in 2017-18. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘It was all of us’: Khawaja blows the whistle on more sandpaper use in South Africa in 2018 Where Smith and Warner were able to return to the Test side for long stints, adding considerably to their records and pay packets, Bancroft has never been able to do anything that would shake the most indelible images of him – a cricketer shoving sandpaper down his underpants in a moment of panic in Cape Town. He is to Sandpapergate what Trevor Chappell was to underarm. Bancroft has spoken extensively about how hard he tried to fit into the team. It’s worth noting that he was selected in place of a young Matt Renshaw, who had not fit into the team back then as a 20-year-old.

Advertisement

The coach at the time, Darren Lehmann, liked to refer to Bancroft as “a good kid”, almost as though he was an agreeable character who would do what the team asked of him. In South Africa, that was taken to extremes. Khawaja’s account shows that in Port Elizabeth, after Warner expressed hesitation about using sandpaper due to the amount of public scrutiny he was under from broadcasters, Bancroft put his hand up. At least once during the series, he received a team shout out and a round of applause for what he was doing for the team in “managing” the ball. It is possible that not everyone in the team knew exactly what he was doing with the ball. But there’s little doubt that Bancroft’s job was well known. Cameron Bancroft is questioned by Umpires Richard Illingworth and Nigel Llong during the fateful third Test match at Newlands in 2018. AFP

Advertisement

Khawaja also recounts that a member of the coaching staff entered their segmented part of the Newlands dressing room on the fateful day the scandal was exposed, encouraging Bancroft to do more of what he was doing. Once again, the compulsion to fit in would have been overwhelming. So Bancroft raised the degree of risk, from a brief bit of ball management on the boundary at the start of a session, to trying to continue doing so in the middle of the ground, by the pitch, under the full glare of the SuperSport cameras. The rest followed painfully. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket Bancroft considers breaking silence as Khawaja reveals promise behind sandpaper claims In December 2018, when his ban was about to expire, Bancroft sat down for a Fox Cricket interview with Adam Gilchrist. That interview was expected to be the moment at which Bancroft spoke expansively about what had happened in South Africa, who did what, and when. But instead, the desire to fit back in took precedence, and he spoke in generalities about his journey of self-realisation. “The decision was based around my values at the time,” he told Gilchrist. “I valued fitting in. With fitting in, you hope that earns you respect.

Advertisement

“If I’d actually said no, and went to bed that night ... I would’ve gone to bed and felt like I would’ve let everybody down. I would’ve felt like I let the team down.” Three years later, when interviewed by The Guardian’s sports writer Donald McRae, Bancroft was pushed harder on collective knowledge and responsibility. This led to his admission that it was “self-explanatory” that the bowlers would have known they were operating with a tampered ball. Bancroft’s words pushed Khawaja to the edge of making his own public admissions about the matter. The bowlers, both in 2021 and again now through Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc, have maintained that they did not know. The specifics of those denials, and also multiple lapses in recall, have been the subject of much debate since Khawaja spoke about the affair ahead of his book release. Steven Smith and Cameron Bancroft in 2018. Getty Bancroft is aware of what Cummins has said, in addition to the very different recollections of Khawaja, Warner and the tour squad member Chadd Sayers. He must have collected his thoughts to consider how closely, or otherwise, they chime with those accounts.

Advertisement

The memories of Bancroft may be the key to ending an exhausting couple of weeks of claim and counter-claim. He has sat with those thoughts in his head for a long time, including specific conversations with numerous figures both before and after the fateful moment he was captured on the big screen at Newlands. Bancroft’s version of events would doubtless be painful for some, but that must be balanced against the weight of experience that had caused his shoulders to regularly sag over the past eight years. As the old saying goes, the truth hurts, but silence kills. Bancroft clearly felt a little less suffocated when he reached three figures in Adelaide. Collingwood is bringing back the long-retired No.42 of their late premiership hero Darren Millane, awarding that famed number to their first draft choice annually. The Magpies will begin by handing the number to their first-round choice in Thursday’s national draft, and will continue to award that jumper each year to their first draft pick, with the player who adorns the number swapping to a different jumper in his second year. Darren Millane No.42 has been brought out of retirement by Collingwood. Julian Kingma Millane died in a car accident in the post-season of 1991, aged 26, barely 12 months after he was a key figure in Collingwood’s drought-busting premiership. His number was retired by the Magpies after his death. Collingwood had considered restoring the number during Eddie McGuire’s long stint as president, but the Magpies chose to keep the jumper retired in consideration of the Millane family’s wishes.

Advertisement

Collingwood chief executive Craig Kelly, who was a premiership teammate and close friend of Millane’s, said the return of No.42 provided players, staff and the club’s fan base the opportunity to learn Millane’s story and “ensure the values he embodied are passed on to future generations”. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Who will your AFL club draft? Our expert prediction of the first round The awarding of No.42 to the first player drafted each season repeats Collingwood’s brief tradition of handing the first draftee No.35, the number worn by full-back Simon Prestigiacomo and (most famously) and club legend Peter Daicos. That ritual ceased when Collingwood recruited Nick Daicos, the champion younger son of Peter Daicos, who took ownership of the number. Kelly thanked the Millane family – his mother Denise, brothers John and Sean and their children – for their support in restoring the jumper. “As promised to the family, the Millane name will remain the only name on that locker, which is an important part of why the number will rotate,” Kelly said.

Advertisement

A skilful and physically imposing wingman and midfielder, Millane was a cornerstone of Collingwood’s rise under Leigh Matthews and in the premiership of 1990, when he was awarded the AFL Players’ Association MVP (later named after his coach), was an All Australian and, most famously, played the entire finals series with a broken thumb. Darren Millane was integral to Collingwood’s premiership in 1990. Fairfax Media As an aggressive and powerful player who instilled both fear in the opposition and reassurance in teammates, Millane was adored by the Collingwood army, not least for his larrikin qualities. His death from a drink-driving accident, in which he was intoxicated, was met with an outpouring of grief in the football world. Originally from Noble Park, Millane was an immediate gun when he arrived at Collingwood in 1984 from VFA club Dandenong, having been spurned by Hawthorn and St Kilda. He won the club best and fairest in 1987, was runner-up in 1990, and named in Collingwood’s team of the century. He played 147 games. Kelly said football brought people together “from all walks of life and different backgrounds ... there are important lessons from Darren’s time at Collingwood, his life and his passing that we must continue to share with our players and staff”.

Advertisement

Denise Millane said while seeing her son’s No.42 retired was a great honour for the family, “we’re equally proud to see it return and be worn by a new young player each season”. “The idea that young players will have the opportunity to wear No.42 and learn about Darren’s values, his teammates and his love for Collingwood is incredibly special for our family.” Collingwood president Barry Carp said Millane held “a very special place in that [Collingwood] history and his contribution to our club will never be forgotten”. The stature of Millane at Collingwood is personified by one of the club’s most earthy coterie groups, Club 42, which was established in honour of the star wingman. In deciding to restore No.42, Collingwood sought recollections from Matthews, former football general manager Graeme Allan, teammate and close mate Denis Banks and McGuire.
