title: How infamous fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried missed out on a $52 billion jackpot
text:
Advertisement

BusinessCompaniesWall Street How infamous fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried missed out on a $52 billion jackpot David Yaffe-Bellany November 17, 2026 — 6:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Sam Bankman-Fried, the convicted cryptocurrency fraudster, lives in a 30-person unit at the federal prison in Lompoc, California, a barbed-wire compound about a million miles away from his former life as a technology billionaire in the Bahamas. For the most part, Bankman-Fried, 34, tries not to think about all the “could-have-beens,” he said on a recent call. But one has become difficult to ignore. Before FTX filed for bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried was worth an estimated $US24 billion, giving him tremendous influence in business and politics. AP In late 2021, the heyday of his FTX crypto exchange, Bankman-Fried spent $US500 million ($742 million) on a 13.5 per cent stake in a little-known artificial intelligence startup called Anthropic. This week, Anthropic is set for an initial public offering that is expected to value the company at $US1.4 trillion, potentially one of the largest Wall Street debuts in history. At that valuation, Bankman-Fried’s investment, diluted over several years, would now be worth an eye-watering $US35 billion — about the size of FTX’s entire business at its peak.

Advertisement

But the shares are gone. They were tied up in bankruptcy court until 2024, when executives overseeing the scattered remains of FTX sold the Anthropic stake for $US1.34 billion — a tiny fraction of its current value. Related Article Review This film was supposed to expose the truth. Instead, it leaves us in a hall of mirrors For Anthropic, the fate of those shares is an odd quirk of history. For Bankman-Fried, it’s a source of extreme frustration and resentment. Even after a fraud conviction, a failed appeal and a succession of public humiliations, he is still trying to prove his innocence, arguing that FTX had sufficient resources to avoid bankruptcy. “There’s no point in obsessing over regrets,” he said. “But it’s certainly something that I’ve spent, despite that, a fair bit of time thinking through.” In September, Bankman-Fried submitted the longest of long-shot appeals to the Supreme Court, where he cited the Anthropic investment. He claimed that the judge in his trial had improperly prevented him from arguing that FTX had enough money to repay its users.

Advertisement

But none of his arguments was ever likely to overcome the basic facts of FTX’s collapse, an epic financial fraud that drew instant comparisons to Bernie Madoff’s Ponzi scheme. Bankman-Fried gave up control of FTX in November 2022, after a run on deposits exposed an $US8 billion hole in customer accounts. A year later, he was convicted on seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. He had used the missing money to buy luxury real estate, donate to political campaigns and invest in startups like Anthropic. Ultimately, the return on those investments proved irrelevant, as far as guilt and innocence were concerned. In US District Court for the Southern District of New York, Judge Lewis A. Kaplan memorably compared Bankman-Fried to a “thief who takes his loot to Las Vegas and successfully bets the stolen money.” He sentenced him to 25 years in prison. Anthropic is set to list on Wall Street this week. Michael Nagle “Mr. Bankman-Fried conveniently skips over the fact that he misappropriated and gambled with customer moneys,” John Ray, a corporate turnaround expert who oversaw the bankruptcy, said in a statement. “We are proud of the integrity and impact of the work we have done with our large team of committed professionals.” A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment.

Advertisement

Before FTX filed for bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried was worth an estimated $US24 billion, giving him tremendous influence in business and politics. His company was one of the world’s largest crypto exchanges, a venue where customers could buy, sell and store digital coins. Bankman-Fried was also a leading practitioner of “effective altruism,” a philanthropic movement that focuses on combating threats that might emerge decades or centuries in the future. Like many effective altruists, Bankman-Fried was concerned about the dangers of out-of-control AI long before it became a major talking point in American politics. Those views aligned him with Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, who moved in the same effective altruist circles. Amodei started the AI company after leaving a rival, OpenAI, in late 2020 amid disagreements over how to make the technology safer. Bankman-Fried said he spoke with Amodei not long after that, when FTX was based in Hong Kong. “I was one degree removed and knew a number of people who knew him,” Bankman-Fried recalled. Amodei struck him as “really intelligent, dedicated, very knowledgeable.” In April 2022, Anthropic announced the investment from Bankman-Fried and two of his FTX colleagues, drawing little notice at the time.

Advertisement

“We cared about AI companies being responsible, and preparing for AI to help rather than hurt society,” Bankman-Fried said on the phone from prison. “Anthropic seemed far more committed to that than the other major companies.” Related Article Entrepreneur ‘Lies and forgeries’: Forbes 30 under 30 star jailed over $10 million fraud Then in fall 2022, FTX plunged into crisis, exposing a giant theft of customer money. Three weeks later, OpenAI released its ChatGPT chatbot, setting off an AI frenzy. Within a year, Bankman-Fried had been convicted, while Anthropic was raising billions of dollars from high-profile investors like Amazon. It had recently released a popular chatbot, Claude. As Anthropic turned into one of Silicon Valley’s hottest startups, the fate of Bankman-Fried’s shares became a subject of intense debate in Delaware bankruptcy court.

Advertisement

When FTX failed, Bankman-Fried had handed control to Ray, who had managed the unwinding of Enron. Working with the law firm Sullivan & Cromwell, Ray set out to raise funds to pay back FTX customers in full. Bankman-Fried had left a messy assortment of corporate assets, including obscure digital coins, properties in the Bahamas and shares in other companies. Ray’s team started looking for buyers. A wide-ranging sale is typical in any corporate bankruptcy, where the job of the estate is to maximise recoveries as efficiently as possible. But some customers wanted FTX to sit on the Anthropic stake for longer. “I wish they held onto it,” said Sunil Kavuri, an FTX customer who testified at Bankman-Fried’s sentencing. “I foresaw that it would be one of the most valuable assets.” It didn’t help that Ray came across as misinformed about the potential value of the shares. In an interview with author Michael Lewis, he dismissed the company as “this thing called Anthropic.” “It’s just a bunch of people with an idea,” Ray said. “Nothing.”

Advertisement

In the end, FTX sold the Anthropic stake at about $US30 per share to a few dozen investors, who paid $US1.34 billion, according to court filings. The buyers included a business entity linked to Mubadala, the United Arab Emirates investment fund; the nonprofit Ford Foundation; and the trading firm Jane Street, which once employed Bankman-Fried. A spokesperson for the FTX estate said the sale of the Anthropic stake was “conducted through a court-supervised process and achieved market value at the time”. The collapse of FTX sent shockwaves through the world of crypto. AP “Billions of stolen funds were misappropriated and invested, without customer consent,” the spokesperson said. “There was no way to know at that time whether those investments would succeed or fail and many did fail.” Representatives for Jane Street and the Ford Foundation declined to comment. Mubadala did not respond to a request for comment.

Advertisement

A bankruptcy estate has significant leeway to decide when and how to sell its assets. Under the circumstances, FTX’s handling of the Anthropic shares was reasonable, said Lindsey Simon, a professor at Emory University School of Law. “At the time, there was no news about an IPO,” Simon said. “Now we know that they became extraordinarily valuable. But what if they had turned into nothing?” Even after a fraud conviction, a failed appeal and a succession of public humiliations, he is still trying to prove his innocence, arguing that FTX had sufficient resources to avoid bankruptcy. In May 2024, the estate announced that FTX’s creditors were set to receive as much as $US1.18 for every dollar they lost when the exchange failed — more than a full repayment. But that has not quieted the complaints. The promised returns were pegged to the value of crypto at the time FTX collapsed, when the market was in a deep slump. If customers held bitcoin on FTX on the day the company filed for bankruptcy, they would be compensated in line with the coin’s price at that moment — not its current price, which is several times higher.

Advertisement

“It was our money, and we didn’t give him rights to use our money,” Kavuri said. “It sucks.” Related Article Billionaires ‘Screw with me’: America’s richest prisoner opens up These days, Bankman-Fried has only limited contact with the outside world. He exchanges messages with a network of journalists, friends and relatives, who have kept him up-to-date on AI developments. Bankman-Fried can access the prison phones for 15 minutes at a time, before each call automatically ends. Over several conversations this fall, he kept returning to Ray and the bankruptcy lawyers. “I’m sure you could’ve come up with a way for them to manage it worse,” he said, “but I can’t think of one off the top of my head.”

Advertisement

Bankman-Fried was repeating grievances that have been repeatedly rejected in court. But does he ever ponder an alternate universe where FTX didn’t implode and the Anthropic shares made him incredibly wealthy? “A little bit,” he said, starting to answer. “I try not to spend too much time. …” Then the call cut out. title: Minns auctions off his credibility with pause on underquoting laws
text:

NationalNSWProperty prices Editorial Minns auctions off his credibility with pause on underquoting laws The Herald's View Editorial November 17, 2026 — 5:49pm

November 17, 2026 — 5:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Since auctions became the favourite game in town, purchasing a house in Sydney has developed into a one-sided affair in which sellers and real estate agents hold all the cards, and buyers enter the lion’s den at their peril. The Minns government last June introduced a suite of reform legislation to restore some transparency for buyers following a Herald investigation that uncovered rampant underquoting by real estate agents. This masthead found almost half of all property sales at auction in Sydney sold for more than 10 per cent above the guide. The sale price section of the reform raised alarms in the property industry. Peter Rae The reforms promised five-fold increased penalties and mandated price guides on all advertising. It also pledged a statement of information backing the estimated sales price to ensure “buyers know accurate pricing by requiring online ads to be updated within one business day if a displayed price no longer complies with the law. For example, if the estimated selling price is revised, a written offer is rejected because it’s too low or the property is passed in at auction”. It was the sale price section that raised alarms in the property industry.

Advertisement

The changes were eminently reasonable in a boom, but with a market downturn and sellers holding out for yesteryear’s prices, estate agents faced the possibility that if they rejected an offer, then ended up cutting a price guide for an unsold property, they risked breaching the letter of the law. The industry warned the Minns government on October 22, but Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong rejected the concerns, saying the laws would benefit buyers and agencies. Then, out of the blue on Monday, Minns hit the pause button. He said the reforms had been raised by real estate agents in his Kogarah electorate, who were concerned restrictions would further undermine trade amid a sharp downturn. The reforms were only hours from taking effect. They’ve now been deferred for 12 months. Minns and Chanthivong both went to ground on Tuesday. Police Minister Yasmin Catley and Attorney General Michael Daley refused to answer questions about whom the government consulted before shelving the legislation.

Advertisement

Minns’ backflip – after real estate companies had poured resources into complying with the laws and buyers had been primed to expect greater transparency from Tuesday – has not been satisfactorily explained. Related Article Analysis

Bidding blind Dodgy real estate agents are the only winners from Minns’ policy debacle Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the laws had been designed for a market “galloping ahead in price” rather than falling, but this explanation raises questions about why the government would design laws only for a rising market (history shows that even NSW’s ballooning house prices fall every few years). His rationale also fails to explain why all the reforms were shelved rather than simply the one that legitimately concerned the industry. Governments and the industry have made billions from Sydney’s real estate boom.

Advertisement

The reforms were supposed to deliver greater transparency for those who bear the brunt of all-too-common deceptions. The result of Monday’s decision is that home buyers who have suffered from the manipulative tactics of unscrupulous agents will not be better protected. The premier’s U-turn on his promise is reprehensible. Buyers who attend auctions across Sydney in the coming weeks may wonder, understandably, why the laws were shelved. Instead, nothing has changed, and they’ve been left as easy prey to an industry that has shown few qualms about using underquoting as a carrot to buyers. title: What we know about the planned Rwanda migrant deportation centre
text:
In brief The initiative was taken by Austria, Germany, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands.

Nationals of any country are eligible, according to those involved in the plan.

Five European Union (EU) countries overnight announced a plan to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, the first such facility outside the bloc.

Here is what we know about the "return-hub" initiative by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands.

Who will be deported and how?

The five nations have been exploring sending migrants to centres outside Europe for months, with the pilot project planned to be launched next year.

During a joint press announcement in Vienna, ministers from the five EU countries and Rwanda remained evasive on the project's scope.

But according to people involved, the centre will house around 100 migrants.

They will be men and women whose asylum applications have been rejected but who refuse to return to their countries of origin, despite having exhausted all avenues of appeal.

According to those involved in the plan, nationals of any country will be eligible to be sent to the facility, although minors would be excluded.

National authorities from the five European countries' national authorities will be responsible for transferring rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

Non-governmental refugee and humanitarian organisations are worried the initiative could ultimately target all asylum seekers — a claim denied by the five countries involved.

What conditions will migrants face in Rwanda?

Once they arrive in Rwanda, authorities of the east African country will take charge of them, and they will receive residence permits.

They will be placed in a centre, which Rwandan authorities referred to as a "welcome centre".

The five European countries insist that it will be open, without any deprivation of liberty or barbed wire.

READ MORE Tony Burke announces backpacker visa backdown after industry pressure

A site has already been identified. The European countries, however, have refused to specify where it is.

They only stress that it is not one of the centres the United Kingdom had planned to use.

London had announced plans in 2022 to send asylum seekers to Rwanda, but the project was ultimately abandoned because of legal obstacles.

How long will the migrants stay at the centre?

The idea is for the migrants to stay in the centre for a few months, with the aim that they then integrate into Rwandan society.

"These illegal migrants who will be relocated to Rwanda are not going to be kept in a camp or in a dedicated area. They will be integrated in our society," Rwandan interior minister Vincent Biruta told the press conference in Vienna.

Vocational training and language courses are to be offered to them.

The five EU countries also say an independent monitoring mechanism — the details of which have not been spelled out — will be put in place to ensure respect for human rights.

Another option is for the exiles to return voluntarily to their country of origin, but not to the EU.

Is the move legal?

Those involved in the plan hope it will discourage migrants from trying to settle on the European continent, besides getting those asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected out of the EU.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the project aimed to send a "signal ... that you can no longer enter the European Union illegally and think that you can just stay around".

The EU states have refused to say what Rwanda would receive in return.

The five countries claim that the legal basis is solid, relying on relevant EU legislation adopted a few months ago.

They have dismissed fierce criticism and concern about the treatment of migrants.

The plans are expected to face court challenges.

title: One Nation, Greens weigh in after Qld and NT reject medical guidance on puberty blockers
text:
In Brief National advice has recommended puberty blockers as a possible part of treatment for young trans people under several conditions.

Public hospitals in both Queensland and the NT are prohibited from prescribing puberty blockers to children under 18.

New advice from Australia's independent medical council recommending puberty blockers for teenage trans and gender diverse people, in limited cases, will be ignored in Queensland and the Northern Territory, and One Nation says it will not support the treatment nationally or if elected in Victoria.

Meanwhile, the federal government, Opposition and Greens all welcomed the advice.

The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) released interim advice on Monday that, as part of a shared decision between a young person, their parents or carers, and their doctors, puberty blockers can be considered if the young person has reached puberty and is assessed as suitable. The treatment is reversible.

Health Minister Mark Butler told Channel Nine on Tuesday that the public debate concerned a relatively small group of very vulnerable young people who are over-represented in mental health and suicide statistics.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He argued that the issue should be referred to the Australian health and medical research body "rather than have debate settled by commentators in our big newspapers".

Butler also defended the research behind the guidelines, which found a low level of certainty for better mental health outcomes for trans and gender diverse teenagers who accessed puberty blockers.

"It's not unusual to have guidelines indicate a level of low certainty around evidence. More recently, I've seen that in pregnancy care guidelines, dementia care guidelines, arthritis, and even stroke management as well," Butler said.

Equality Australia welcomed the guidance on Monday, with CEO Anna Brown saying it "reinforces that the care trans young people are receiving in Australia today is grounded in evidence, informed by clinical expertise and guided by the individual needs of young people".

Why have Queensland and the NT rejected the guidance?

The Queensland and Northern Territory governments immediately rejected the NHMRC advice on Monday, insisting they will maintain their bans based on their own reviews of the evidence.

Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls said the state had already conducted its own independent review and that the NHMRC's advice won't change its decision.

The state introduced a ban on public hospitals prescribing any gender-affirming hormone treatments in January 2025, following research in the United Kingdom by paediatrician Hilary Cass.

The Cass review of youth gender identity services in the UK found the international and local evidence base supporting early puberty suppression for minors with gender dysphoria or gender incongruence is "remarkably weak" and lacked long-term data on clinical effectiveness or safety.

READ MORE Kyro wanted gender-affirming treatment but was told he had to wait to make the decision

Butler said Queensland's own review didn't have the status, scope, or "purpose" of the council, and the UK review was influenced by "questionable private prescribing practices" that do not occur in Australia.

The biggest local gender clinic, in Melbourne, prescribed puberty blockers to an average of eight young people over eight years, with wait times for treatment averaging 530 days, Butler said.

Nicholls said the state's position "remains unchanged and we will continue to prioritise the health, safety and wellbeing of young Queenslanders".

Queensland's ban was briefly overturned by the Supreme Court last year, but Nicholls used ministerial powers to immediately reinstate it hours after the court's decision.

The NT government also said in a statement that its ban will remain in place.

A spokesperson for the Northern Territory government told Nine Newspapers that its decision is consistent with those of Queensland, the United Kingdom and Finland, "which have all taken a cautious approach".

Labor ordered the NHMRC review into the prescription of gender-affirming hormones for young people two days after the Queensland government's 2025 ban.

The new guidelines do not require a child to be diagnosed with gender dysphoria, which is psychological distress caused when someone's gender identity does not align with the sex they were assigned at birth.

What have others said?

Greens leader David Shoebridge told SBS News Australia should be taking the best advice from the best experts.

"This seems like a very credible policy that's been considered not by politicians who are trying to make a political point, but by the medical experts," Shoebridge said. "I think the more we listen to the medical and ethical experts, and the less we listen to the likes of the NT chief minister or the Queensland premier in this space, the more the country will be on the right track."

Liberal senator Andrew Bragg told Channel Nine on Tuesday the transgender community should not be used as a "political football".

"I think there are people in politics who've used them [as] part of their kind of hate campaign," Bragg said. "They are a tiny minority, and we should be kind to one another. We've got to live and let live ethos in this country."

The senator said decisions about gender-affirming treatment were, for the most part, "not judgements children should be making", but said there were rare circumstances in which accessing puberty blockers would be appropriate for a child's health.

A One Nation spokesperson said it would fight to ban the treatment if elected in Victoria or federally.

The federal Coalition noted the new advice deviates from the UK Cass review and does not require a gender dysphoria diagnosis.

The advice is open for public comment until 18 January, with clinical guidelines, beyond the use of puberty suppressants, developed "probably into 2028", Butler said.

title: Tony Burke announces backpacker visa backdown after industry pressure
text:
In brief Labor announced a plan earlier this year to significantly reduce third-year working holiday visas to 5,000.

Tony Burke says that figure will now be 25,000, while extending regional work requirements for second-year working holidaymakers.

After viral videos, threats of harvests being left to wither and fears from the Labor backbench, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has agreed to some concessions over his backpacker visa crackdown.

Despite announcing a major reduction for third-year working holiday visas to just 5,000 earlier this year, Burke has announced Labor will lift that number to 25,000.

Those who are successful will still be chosen through a ballot system.

"These changes give businesses and working holidaymakers clear rules and time to plan, while making sure the program continues to support the regions and industries that rely on it," Burke told reporters in Cairns on Tuesday.

"Australia will continue to welcome working holidaymakers. These reforms make the program fairer, more targeted and sustainable for the long term."

From March, the number of days working holidaymakers will need to complete in the regions to be eligible for a second year will increase from 88 to 120.

"This creates a very significant shift, but also means for the people who are wanting to qualify for their second year, we're getting more regional days out of them," Burke said.

Burke announced a raft of migration changes, including the backpacker move, in his address to the National Press Club in September, following delays and concerns from inside Labor.

Labor MPs in regional areas of the Northern Territory and Queensland have also been facing direct lobbying about the threat of a diminishing workforce.

Labor backbencher Matt Smith said on Tuesday he had led a delegation of Far North Queensland industry leaders to Canberra to help "guide the shape of those reforms".

Burke targeted the backpacker numbers as part of his attempt to ensure the government doesn't overshoot its net overseas migration (NOM) targets.

The NOM has become a major focus of political attacks from One Nation and the Opposition, which have accused the government of failing to manage migration and allowing numbers to balloon without adequate housing.

Coalition urges Labor to 'axe' ballot

Following Burke's announcement, Opposition leader Angus Taylor criticised the government's proposed ballot system for second and third-year working holiday visas.

"They should just axe it," Taylor told reporters in Townsville, adding that the Coalition would "absolutely" repeal the system if elected.

Burke said the Opposition's proposed immigration policy — which would remove caps on second and third-year working holiday visas — would cut temporary migration numbers without affecting "the areas where they are really needed".

The government says the changes announced on Tuesday won’t affect the overall NOM projections, which Labor wants to bring down from 245,000 this financial year to 225,000 next year.

Australia is still negotiating with the United Kingdom over changing the free trade deal that has exempted British working holidaymakers from working in regional areas.

Burke said discussions are underway to reach an agreement with the UK that would mean a "different sort of obligation than what is currently there for UK backpackers" and said talks had been promising.

title: Fake websites, fraudulent listings: The tactics scammers are using to target travellers
text:

Smartraveller has issued a warning to Australians ahead of the holiday season, with scammers looking to take advantage of tourists.

title: The 'missing piece' in Australia's fight against an enduring addiction
text:
in brief The number of illicit tobacco products has dropped, while the number of smokers continues to fall.

Experts and advocates say there needs to be a shift in the retail environment to further reduce smoking and illegal products.

Australia's illicit tobacco market has shrunk for the first time in years, according to new government data. However, experts say the crackdown is missing a crucial measure: restricting where tobacco products can be sold.

Data from the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commission (ITEC) has revealed a 24 per cent drop in the volume of contraband product in circulation over the past financial year.

While the exact size of the black-market sector cannot be calculated, it is estimated to have shrunk by as much as 1,438 tonnes.

It follows five years of significant growth in the amount of illegal tobacco available on the market.

At the same time, there has been a downward trend in the number of Australians smoking, but of those who do use tobacco, a growing number are using illicit products.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Becky Freeman, a tobacco control expert at the University of Sydney, said the data suggests a "changing of the tide" in the fight against illicit tobacco, but that more needs to be done.

Freeman said the widespread availability of cigarettes and vapes at supermarkets and convenience stores contributed to the use of both illicit and legal tobacco products.

Tobacco use carries serious health risks and is a leading cause of preventable illness and death.

"We’ve never questioned that this deadly product should just be sold absolutely everywhere in every single community all across the country. And to me, that’s the missing piece that could really tackle this issue," she told SBS News.

READ MORE The dramatic shift in a longstanding Australian addiction

By reducing the availability of cigarettes, it could lead to fewer people taking up smoking to begin with, who may go on to later buy illicit tobacco products.

Vendors must hold a valid state or territory tobacco licence for each physical premises or online store where tobacco or non-tobacco smoking products are sold.

Illicit tobacco on the decline, government says, as excise revenue falls

ITEC estimates the total volume of black-market tobacco has fallen to 5,893 tonnes and could be as low as 4,453 tonnes.

Source: SBS News

The government said the decline was due to stronger enforcement, larger seizures, and better coordination among federal, state and territory agencies.

But Freeman said enforcement is only one part of the solution to stopping the illicit tobacco trade.

She told SBS News that the product is too easy to access, with smokers able to go to a convenience store "with ease" and pay less for an illicit product than for an approved one.

"It's your local friendly shopkeeper who will sell you these products. And so they just kind of go, 'oh, well, you know, they're willing to sell them to me. It can't be that bad.'"

'No time to ease up'

The decline in black market tobacco products, combined with fewer smokers, is welcome news to the Australian Council of Smoking and Health (ACOSH).

Its CEO Laura Hunter told SBS News the government should continue to ramp up its efforts to stop the illicit trade.

Source: SBS News

"We need to keep disrupting the trade at every point in the supply chain. We need to disrupt it before it reaches Australia, at the border, and in the communities where it's sold," she said.

"It's no time to ease up."

Addressing the "retail environment" around where tobacco is sold is key, she added, saying "there is an incredibly high number of tobacco retailers".

Australia has around 40,000 retailers that are selling tobacco products legally, according to ACOSH.

The country has about 9,500 supermarkets and roughly 7,000 petrol stations, meaning tobacco is far more widely available than everyday grocery or fuel items.

SBS News asked the federal government whether it would consider restricting which vendors could sell tobacco products, given the number of vendors compared to supermarkets and petrol stations.

Staff for Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill pointed to a speech he delivered in March.

"That imbalance raises questions about whether tobacco products should instead be sold only through mixed‑use retail settings, subject to stricter licensing, oversight and compliance. Interesting questions for the future," Hill said in an excerpt.

Retail licensing of tobacco falls solely within the remit of states and territories.

The missing piece in combating tobacco

Freeman argued that reducing the number of vendors permitted to sell tobacco products could curb the sale of illicit cigarettes and vapes.

"Tobacco shops are literally everywhere. Any sort of store can sell you cigarettes," she said.

"And to really get on top of this issue, we have got to start ramping that down. We need fewer places selling cigarettes, which would help with enforcement efforts as well."

Source: SBS News

Coral Gartner, a tobacco control expert at the University of Queensland, agreed that the tobacco product supply chain needs stronger governance.

"This is a really harmful product that's addictive. And the way that it's been allowed to be sold in stores is not the way that we regulate other harmful addictive products," she told SBS News.

Gartner said that health campaigns around the dangers of smoking have been effective in reducing smoking rates. However, she wants to see more support for cessation programs.

"In Queensland they've got some great programs where if you meet certain criteria, you can get free nicotine replacement therapy sent to you, along with support counselling," she said.

Gartner wants to see programs like that rolled out permanently nationwide.

Tobacco excise revenue, a tax on tobacco products, fell to about $4.1 billion in the 2026 financial year, down sharply from a record high of $16.3 billion in 2020.

Meanwhile, the government reported that the illicit tobacco trade cost between $7.7 billion and $11.8 billion in potential revenue in the 2024–2025 financial year alone.

"This reduces revenue that can fund the public health system in treating smoking-related illnesses," the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026 reads.

title: A plan to keep more of Australia's gas onshore faces a constitutional problem
text:
In brief Labor's gas reservation plan faces Senate roadblocks over design, WA inclusion and ministerial powers.

Coalition, Greens and crossbench have opposed the bill over investment risks, tax demands and climate concerns.

The Albanese government wants to push down gas prices by engineering a "modest oversupply" of gas but a proposed reservation scheme is deadlocked in the Senate due to disagreements over its design.

The proposed rules to force liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporters to pump more gas to Australians are problematic for the industry, the Coalition and the Greens said, for different reasons, including whether they encourage or discourage new supply.

The government needs the backing of either the Greens or the Coalition to pass the bill, as manufacturing unions urge the Senate to pass it before the end of the year.

The laws would create a Domestic Supply Obligation (DSO) to force big LNG exporters to reserve and supply up to 20 per cent of their annual export energy to Australians as calculated by the Australian Energy Regulator (AER), starting in 2028.

The AER will forecast domestic demand, add a 10 per cent market oversupply buffer, subtract non-exporter supply, and spread the remaining amount across LNG exporters.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Resources Minister Madeleine King said the policy will shield households, gas-powered electricity generators, and local manufacturers from international price spikes and domestic shortfalls.

A national scheme, with a single-state exception

For the law to be constitutional, it must apply to all states, but Australia has two disconnected gas markets. Western Australia's pipelines don't connect to the east coast because they don't run across the Great Sandy Desert and the Nullarbor Plain.

King acknowledged the issue and said the law allows DSO for the Western Australian market to be set at zero, or very low levels.

The Coalition and WA gas industry want a carve-out from the rules but Labor is only allowing adjustments through a ministerial decision. King argued that including WA helps make the scheme constitutionally robust.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told reporters on Monday: "Our position is very clear that WA shouldn't be in it because they don't have the problem we have on the east coast".

"We do not need WA being part of this scheme," Taylor said. "WA says that. The WA premier says that, so sort it out. It's pretty simple."

Grattan Energy and Climate Change deputy program director Hamish McKenzie told SBS News that a WA parliamentary inquiry found exporters were "significantly under-delivering gas".

READ MORE Australian gas giant and Traditional Owners locked in $300 million compensation battle

"The brutal reality is that the state gas reservation in WA is full of holes," McKenzie said.

"The federal scheme is much, much stronger, and if it was applied in WA, it would probably result in substantially more of West Australia's gas being kept onshore for West Australian users.

"Gas producers don't want that, and they are running a campaign to make sure that WA is exempt."

Ministerial powers queried

The minister's power to reduce or exclude gas companies' obligations from the scheme is controversial because one of the three east coast exporters — Gladstone LNG — has signed contracts to export much more gas than its planned production until at least 2036.

If a company's obligations under the new law require them to break an export contract and if they take "active steps" to try to deliver domestic gas, they may be excused.

"The minister of the day has a huge amount of discretion as to how they will implement the reservation," McKenzie said.

There aren't a lot of guardrails around the minister's ability to dictate supply and waive obligations, he said.

"The thing that should really be fixed is probably not the fine details of how it will be applied, but the circumstances in which the minister can actually use that discretion."

Stuffing a golden gas goose with oversupply?

The minister can set an "oversupply" percentage, between 0 and 10 per cent of demand, which is the "biggest problem with the legislation", McKenzie said.

"Forcing 10 per cent more supply into the market than is demanded every year risks massively tanking the price, putting unviable pressure on domestic gas producers in a way that could, after a couple of years, leave the east coast gas market even more reliant on the exported sea gas supply, which is actually the opposite of what the reservation is trying to do," he said.

Taylor told reporters on Monday that to get prices down, you need more supply, and you won't have more supply if you trash the industry.

"So, they will push too much supply into the [Australian] market, but we need investment," Taylor said.

"We need to see a price that's going to get the investment, as well as the price to consumers, industrial and household, small business. That is achievable whilst we're still getting the investment."

Australia must produce more gas, not simply shuffle existing supplies around, Opposition resources spokesperson senator Susan McDonald said.

"Labor’s proposal in its current form will drive away investment, destroy domestic-only producers, discourage new production and ultimately leave Australians with less gas and higher prices.

No reservations for the Greens or crossbench

The Greens won't support the bill unless it includes a 25 per cent tax on gas exports. Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May said the government should "do a deal for everyday Australians, not for gas donors", warning the new law may make it easier to open new gas fields and "make the climate crisis worse".

Independent senator David Pocock said Australia "needed a better return for its exports" and continues to push for a 25 per cent tax.

"I think it’s a good start, but I’m going to continue to push for a fair return for all Australians and for future generations of Australians on a resource that, once it’s sold, is gone," he told Channel Nine on Monday.

"We’ve got to get better at capturing long-term benefit from the sale of our resources."

King has rejected this, saying nothing gets cheaper after it's taxed.

"We have seen other countries where they do introduce what Senator Pocock has suggested, like a windfall tax, and what that has ended up doing is driving the industry basically away."

title: What Anthony Albanese's fried chicken move could signal to the world
text:
In brief Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has celebrated the upcoming launch of Filipino fast food chain Jollibee in Australia.

Some social media users expressed confusion about a video the prime minister posted supporting the chain.

While Anthony Albanese's promotion of a Filipino fast food chain has raised some eyebrows online, experts say the prime minister's fried chicken meal could strengthen ties with a regional ally.

Filipino fast food giant Jollibee is set to open in Australia — and the prime minister has celebrated the move in Manila with the company's president and CEO Ernesto Tanmantiong.

The chain, well-known in the Philippines for its fried chicken, operates more than 1,600 stores worldwide and aims to open 35 in NSW and Victoria over five years.

The Australian outlets are expected to create 900 direct jobs.

Albanese, who is in Manila for the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), said he wants to see "more businesses choose Australia as a place to grow and succeed".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He welcomed Jollibee as a "great example of the cultural connections that strengthen our relationship with the Philippines".

More than 400,000 people living in Australia were born in the Philippines, making it the country's fifth-largest diaspora community.

In a video posted to Albanese's Instagram, the prime minister celebrated with Jollibee staff and ate a meal at the fast food chain.

Concern about the PM's post

However, some social media users expressed confusion about the post and Albanese's endorsement of the chain, with one user commenting, "So, are you getting paid for this? Thought it was AI when I first saw it and can't believe it's for real."

Comedian and media personality Ben Sorensen commented on Albanese's video asking: "Was this a sponsored post?"

Politicians highlighting small businesses and large employers around Australia during election periods is extremely common, according to Emily Foley, a research fellow at the University of Canberra.

However, Foley told SBS News she hasn't seen this in a foreign affairs context before.

"I wouldn't say it's particularly common," she said.

Anne Nalder, founder and CEO of the Small Business Association of Australia, told SBS News the prime minister's promotion of Jollibee was "disappointing" at a time when small businesses in the food industry are "barely surviving" due to high costs.

Nalder also noted that around a third of small businesses in Australia are run by migrants.

"There's nothing wrong with an overseas company coming into Australia ... the thing about it is, I would like to see [the prime minister] concentrating on supporting Australian businesses because they need all the support they can get," she said.

A political calculation

Foley said there aren't any rules for politicians that would restrict a post like Albanese's, and his decision to post it likely comes down to a political calculation about appealing to Australia's Filipino diaspora.

"There is a bit of a grappling about what is acceptable for politicians to put on social media and the public sphere, but I don't think there's anything in particular that's necessarily frowned upon [in this case]," Foley said.

Whilst attracting critical comments, Albanese's video also received many supportive responses and attracted over 71,000 likes.

This is also not the first time the prime minister has encouraged a foreign business to enter Australia. During a meeting in the United Arab Emirates in 2025, Albanese visited a Lulu Hypermarket store — one of the largest retail chains in the Middle East, with over 250 stores across the region.

Albanese said at the time he had a discussion with Lulu Hypermarket chair Yusuff Ali as they walked around the store and invited the company to bring more competition to Australia's supermarket sector.

"They are the largest throughout the Middle East. Egypt, here ... the second-largest in Saudi Arabia," Albanese said.

"We know that Aldi, of course, has come to Australia, but this is a significant player that has an engagement with Australia, and I want to see that competition."

However, no plans have been announced for Lulu Hypermarket to enter the Australian market.

Fried chicken diplomacy

On Sunday, the Philippines and Australia signed a defence pact, strengthening ties between the two nations, which have grown over the past decade.

The agreement will step up maritime training and activities amid shared security concerns about China's growing militarisation of the South China Sea, particularly in an area deemed part of Filipino territorial waters by a UN arbitration in 2016.

Australia has taken part in 12 joint patrols with the Philippines in the South China Sea, with four in the last year.

However, Albanese insisted the defence agreement was not aimed specifically at any one country.

"This is about supporting the sovereignty of every country," he said.

While supporting the fried chicken chain is a demonstration of softer diplomacy than a defence pact, emeritus professor Paul Hutchcroft told SBS News the prime minister was likely trying to forge a connection between Australia and the Philippines.

"Jollibee is a source of pride for many Filipinos, competing successfully at home with American fast-food chains while also expanding overseas," he said.

"I can imagine that the PM was tapping into that sense of pride as a way of connecting with citizens of an important Australian ally."

Foley said Albanese's support of Jollibee has "interesting" foreign affairs implications as it highlights a "non-US, non-Western style business that's coming into Australia".

"It obviously speaks to the Labor government's real focus on trying to engage more with the Indo-Pacific, in particular highlighting things like ASEAN centrality — the kind of push to focus more on the political, economic and social ties and connections with neighbouring regional partners, rather than necessarily with the US."

title: What Coles shoppers need to know about the cyber attack on the retailer

The retailer recommended online shoppers update and strengthen their passwords as the hack is investigated.

Australia's second-largest supermarket chain has urged customers to take basic online precautions after it was targeted in a cyber attack.

Coles revealed it was investigating a cyber security incident on Monday morning but said there was no evidence that any data was compromised.

Coles is also investigating reported issues with Liquorland's click-and-collect service.

"We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," Coles said in a statement.

title: 'Light-hearted banter': Anthony Albanese apologises for hot mic comments

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has apologised for joking comments caught on a live mic during a global summit after critics said they hurt Australia’s standing on the world stage.

Albanese was recorded speaking to Energy Minister Chris Bowen while waiting for a round-table discussion to begin at the UN’s COP31 climate summit in Türkiye on Friday.

title: Australians' shifting attitudes towards this emerging technology revealed
text:
in brief The federal goverment is looking to develop AI policy in order to attract investment.

However, plans for major new data centres have recently been paused.

Australians are becoming increasingly wary about artificial intelligence as the use of the technology grows more entrenched.

A report by the Lowy Institute has revealed nearly two-thirds of respondents believe the risks of AI outweigh its benefits.

The October survey found 65 per cent of people were cautious of AI, unchanged from a similar survey in March but well up on the 52 per cent share recorded in 2024.

Some 45 per cent of people previously thought the benefits of AI outweighed the risks to society, but that figure had fallen to 33 per cent in the most recent poll.

It follows a survey carried out by the Pew Research Centre, which found Australians were among the most likely worldwide to say AI concerned them, rather than excited them.

"Australians stand out internationally in their concerns about the technology itself ... these concerns sit against a gloomy economic backdrop," Lowy report author Charles Lyons-Jones said.

"The AI boom is itself part of the picture, with the Reserve Bank flagging that AI-related investment could push up input costs and add to capacity pressures."

A series of plans for major data centres to service AI applications have recently been shelved after community opposition, while the rollout of AI has also been cited for job cuts at large employers such as the big banks.

The release of the report follows the federal government unveiling AI standards that could see tech companies face criminal charges if they fail to prevent harmful conduct.

The measures came in response to an OpenAI agent breaching a Medicare statistics website.

The federal government was looking to develop AI policy in order to get investment from tech companies, but it should proceed with caution, the report noted.

"An emerging risk is that government policy outpaces public sentiment," Lyons-Jones said.

"The strategy asks Australians to host infrastructure for a technology whose risks most of them believe outweigh the benefits."

As the AI race intensifies between the US and China, the report found Australians were more likely to trust technology from American-led firms, such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

Less than a quarter of respondents said they were comfortable with Australian businesses using AI sourced from China, compared with 36 per cent for US firms.

"Some of this discomfort reflects how Australians see the two superpowers," Lyons-Jones said.

"Australians' support for the alliance does not currently extend to American AI. That may change, as public sentiment can swing fast."

title: You may be eligible for a slice of Australia's missing $6 billion superannuation pie
text:
in brief Over three million Australians were reportedly underpaid a collective $6.3 billion in superannuation in 2023-24.

The CEO of the Super Members Council, which is behind that estimate, says "there is much more work to do".

More than $1.1 billion in unpaid superannuation has been returned to Australian workers over the past year, but millions of Australians may still be missing money they are legally owed.

New figures from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) show that the money was returned to the super accounts of more than 900,000 Australians.

The ATO also collected more than $1.1 billion in Super Guarantee Charge liabilities, up from $795 million in the previous financial year.

The enforcement action is encouraging, but the scale of unpaid super remains in the billions of dollars a year, Super Members Council CEO Misha Schubert said.

"Returning more than $1 billion in unpaid super to Australians is welcome progress. This is money owed to working Australians that is finally being paid to them," Schubert said.

"With workers still losing an estimated $6.3 billion in unpaid super a year, there is much more work to do. The onus should not be on everyday Australians to chase the super they are legally owed."

The council estimates that 3.4 million Australians were underpaid $6.3 billion in superannuation during 2023-24, with affected workers missing out on an average of about $1,850 each.

Despite the ATO recovering more than $1.1 billion, the council's analysis suggests it recovers only $1 in every $6 of unpaid super and returns it to workers.

The financial impact can extend well beyond the initial missed payments, with lost investment returns potentially leaving some workers more than $30,000 worse off by retirement.

The council said introducing payday super could help by requiring employers to pay superannuation at the same time as wages.

Super Members Council calls for stronger enforcement

More than 70 per cent of Australians surveyed in a recent poll agreed the reform would help them monitor whether their employer was paying super correctly.

More than half said they would check their super more regularly.

The changes are also expected to give the ATO more timely information to identify potential underpayments and intervene before debts accumulate.

The council is calling for stronger enforcement, including greater use of data matching, proactive investigations, and public targets to recover unpaid super.

It also wants tougher action against employers who deliberately or repeatedly fail to pay super, and to extend the Fair Entitlements Guarantee to cover unpaid super when businesses become insolvent.

Schubert said the focus should now be on identifying unpaid super earlier and ensuring workers receive the money they are owed.

"Payday super is a game changer because it gives workers more visibility and gives the ATO better information to spot missed payments earlier.

"The task now is to make full use of those tools to detect unpaid super early, recover it quickly, and deter it from happening in the first place."

title: Australia defeats New Zealand in both Rugby League World Cup finals
text:
The Kangaroos have defeated New Zealand 32-12, sealing a double victory for Australia, with the Jillaroos earlier annihilating the women's New Zealand side 34-10 in the first instalment of Sunday's Rugby League World Cup finals double-header.

In the men's game, there was an expectation that the Kiwis, searching for their second Cup title and first since 2008, would push Australia all the way after a two-point loss in a pulsating tournament opener.

But the visitors struggled from the outset in Brisbane on Sunday night, with Jamayne Isaako's kick-off floating long in a sign of things to come.

Walsh dazzled at fullback for the Kangaroos, his pace, vision and wicked footwork too much as he helped lay on two tries and generally wreak havoc around the ruck and close to the line.

Conversely, Walsh's New Zealand opposite Kalyn Ponga — International Rugby League's Golden Boot winner on Thursday night — was unable to get into the game.

Australian hooker Harry Grant and halves Tom Dearden and Cam Munster completely outplayed their error-riddled opposites, while the Kangaroos' pack muscled up.

Dearden laid on two first-half tries for Liam Martin with well-timed short balls, while Bradman Best was rewarded for an inspired chase-down tackle of Jahrome Hughes with a try soon after.

When Tom Trbojevic scored to begin the second half, it was 28-6 and effectively game over.

Jack Bostock completed his breakout season with a try in each half for Australia.

It was the Kangaroos' fourth consecutive title and 10th in the last 11 tournaments, dating back to 1975.

Jaime Chapman shines in Jillaroos' victory

In the women's match, Jaime Chapman's explosive first-half hat-trick snuffed out any hope of a New Zealand upset as Australia underlined their women's rugby league dominance with a 34-10 World Cup final annihilation.

The Jillaroos did the damage with six first-half tries on Sunday at Lang Park, with winger Chapman brilliant before the break to cap a historic tournament.

It was Australia's fourth straight Cup triumph, following a 54-4 win in the final four years ago and coming after New Zealand won the first three tournaments between 2000-08.

Chapman carried two players more than 10 metres to score her first, before flying into the corner for another and then busting through four tacklers for a sensational 70-metre solo effort.

That saw her equal the record for tries scored in a World Cup campaign — for men or women — at 13.

But both teams struggled in the Brisbane humidity, with the Ferns' try in the final seconds the only points of an error-riddled second period.

"She's such a great finisher," Australia captain Isabelle Kelly said of Chapman.

"To get that (first try) down with three on her ... that's just Chappo."

For the Jillaroos, there were several poignant narratives to come out of the win.

Coach Jess Skinner's controversial decision to play five-eighth Jesse Southwell and drop Jocelyn Kelleher paid dividends.

Southwell schemed with the ball, landed five goals and was the perfect foil for half Tarryn Aiken, who controlled play with confidence and skill.

Chapman played in the pool games and semi-final in the 2022 World Cup but has now put an indelible stamp on a final.

"There is no better win than winning the World Cup on home turf," she told Channel Seven.

"We connected the first day we came into camp."

Fullback Tamika Upton sat out the tournament four years ago with a calf injury but now the five-time premiership winner has every team accolade in the game to her credit.

All the talk before the clash was the danger posed by New Zealand's Golden Boot winner and strike centre Stacey Waaka.

The former rugby union star, who had scored nine tries in the tournament, was snuffed out by Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly, who confronted Waaka all match and gave her no space.

As the Jillaroos' big guns stood up, centre Jessica Sergis scored her 23rd try in 18 Tests with a 70m dash through the middle off an undetected forward pass.

Aiken turned second-rower Shaylee Bent inside for the second try of the match while Upton started and finished a movement that had her attacking fingerprints all over it.

Ferns fullback Apii Nicholls was her side's best player in a dynamic display until she tore a hamstring in the 66th minute.

When Cameron Bancroft made his first Sheffield Shield century in a year against South Australia at Adelaide Oval two weeks ago, the celebration was meaningful. After cutting a boundary, he sank to his knees with what looked like relief. And not just relief – it was noticeable that a weight appeared to be lifted from his shoulders. Cameron Bancroft. Getty Images The weight had not just been about making hundreds. Australia’s return to South Africa for a first Test series since 2018 had sat very heavily on Bancroft’s shoulders, given that there was always a chance his name would be dragged back into it as the player who used sandpaper on the ball. But ahead of that innings, Bancroft had told those close to him he was informed that Usman Khawaja intended to come forward with his recollections of the Sandpapergate episode, a version of events that showed in detail why there was a case for collective responsibility from the team.

Advertisement

Following a bruising couple of weeks for Australian cricket, Bancroft now has the opportunity to open up with an account that can be more complete than anything yet aired. Though David Warner and Steve Smith both served longer bans, no player was affected more greatly by the scandal than Bancroft. While it is true he briefly returned to the Test team in 2019, the majority of the past eight years have seen him unable to make the kind of mark on the game that would have helped balance what remains a hugely problematic period in the team in 2017-18. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘It was all of us’: Khawaja blows the whistle on more sandpaper use in South Africa in 2018 Where Smith and Warner were able to return to the Test side for long stints, adding considerably to their records and pay packets, Bancroft has never been able to do anything that would shake the most indelible images of him – a cricketer shoving sandpaper down his underpants in a moment of panic in Cape Town. He is to Sandpapergate what Trevor Chappell was to underarm. Bancroft has spoken extensively about how hard he tried to fit into the team. It’s worth noting that he was selected in place of a young Matt Renshaw, who had not fit into the team back then as a 20-year-old.

Advertisement

The coach at the time, Darren Lehmann, liked to refer to Bancroft as “a good kid”, almost as though he was an agreeable character who would do what the team asked of him. In South Africa, that was taken to extremes. Khawaja’s account shows that in Port Elizabeth, after Warner expressed hesitation about using sandpaper due to the amount of public scrutiny he was under from broadcasters, Bancroft put his hand up. At least once during the series, he received a team shout out and a round of applause for what he was doing for the team in “managing” the ball. It is possible that not everyone in the team knew exactly what he was doing with the ball. But there’s little doubt that Bancroft’s job was well known. Cameron Bancroft is questioned by Umpires Richard Illingworth and Nigel Llong during the fateful third Test match at Newlands in 2018. AFP

Advertisement

Khawaja also recounts that a member of the coaching staff entered their segmented part of the Newlands dressing room on the fateful day the scandal was exposed, encouraging Bancroft to do more of what he was doing. Once again, the compulsion to fit in would have been overwhelming. So Bancroft raised the degree of risk, from a brief bit of ball management on the boundary at the start of a session, to trying to continue doing so in the middle of the ground, by the pitch, under the full glare of the SuperSport cameras. The rest followed painfully. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket Bancroft considers breaking silence as Khawaja reveals promise behind sandpaper claims In December 2018, when his ban was about to expire, Bancroft sat down for a Fox Cricket interview with Adam Gilchrist. That interview was expected to be the moment at which Bancroft spoke expansively about what had happened in South Africa, who did what, and when. But instead, the desire to fit back in took precedence, and he spoke in generalities about his journey of self-realisation. “The decision was based around my values at the time,” he told Gilchrist. “I valued fitting in. With fitting in, you hope that earns you respect.

Advertisement

“If I’d actually said no, and went to bed that night ... I would’ve gone to bed and felt like I would’ve let everybody down. I would’ve felt like I let the team down.” Three years later, when interviewed by The Guardian’s sports writer Donald McRae, Bancroft was pushed harder on collective knowledge and responsibility. This led to his admission that it was “self-explanatory” that the bowlers would have known they were operating with a tampered ball. Bancroft’s words pushed Khawaja to the edge of making his own public admissions about the matter. The bowlers, both in 2021 and again now through Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc, have maintained that they did not know. The specifics of those denials, and also multiple lapses in recall, have been the subject of much debate since Khawaja spoke about the affair ahead of his book release. Steven Smith and Cameron Bancroft in 2018. Getty Bancroft is aware of what Cummins has said, in addition to the very different recollections of Khawaja, Warner and the tour squad member Chadd Sayers. He must have collected his thoughts to consider how closely, or otherwise, they chime with those accounts.

Advertisement

The memories of Bancroft may be the key to ending an exhausting couple of weeks of claim and counter-claim. He has sat with those thoughts in his head for a long time, including specific conversations with numerous figures both before and after the fateful moment he was captured on the big screen at Newlands. Bancroft’s version of events would doubtless be painful for some, but that must be balanced against the weight of experience that had caused his shoulders to regularly sag over the past eight years. As the old saying goes, the truth hurts, but silence kills. Bancroft clearly felt a little less suffocated when he reached three figures in Adelaide. Collingwood is bringing back the long-retired No.42 of their late premiership hero Darren Millane, awarding that famed number to their first draft choice annually. The Magpies will begin by handing the number to their first-round choice in Thursday’s national draft, and will continue to award that jumper each year to their first draft pick, with the player who adorns the number swapping to a different jumper in his second year. Darren Millane No.42 has been brought out of retirement by Collingwood. Julian Kingma Millane died in a car accident in the post-season of 1991, aged 26, barely 12 months after he was a key figure in Collingwood’s drought-busting premiership. His number was retired by the Magpies after his death. Collingwood had considered restoring the number during Eddie McGuire’s long stint as president, but the Magpies chose to keep the jumper retired in consideration of the Millane family’s wishes.

Advertisement

Collingwood chief executive Craig Kelly, who was a premiership teammate and close friend of Millane’s, said the return of No.42 provided players, staff and the club’s fan base the opportunity to learn Millane’s story and “ensure the values he embodied are passed on to future generations”. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Who will your AFL club draft? Our expert prediction of the first round The awarding of No.42 to the first player drafted each season repeats Collingwood’s brief tradition of handing the first draftee No.35, the number worn by full-back Simon Prestigiacomo and (most famously) and club legend Peter Daicos. That ritual ceased when Collingwood recruited Nick Daicos, the champion younger son of Peter Daicos, who took ownership of the number. Kelly thanked the Millane family – his mother Denise, brothers John and Sean and their children – for their support in restoring the jumper. “As promised to the family, the Millane name will remain the only name on that locker, which is an important part of why the number will rotate,” Kelly said.

Advertisement

A skilful and physically imposing wingman and midfielder, Millane was a cornerstone of Collingwood’s rise under Leigh Matthews and in the premiership of 1990, when he was awarded the AFL Players’ Association MVP (later named after his coach), was an All Australian and, most famously, played the entire finals series with a broken thumb. Darren Millane was integral to Collingwood’s premiership in 1990. Fairfax Media As an aggressive and powerful player who instilled both fear in the opposition and reassurance in teammates, Millane was adored by the Collingwood army, not least for his larrikin qualities. His death from a drink-driving accident, in which he was intoxicated, was met with an outpouring of grief in the football world. Originally from Noble Park, Millane was an immediate gun when he arrived at Collingwood in 1984 from VFA club Dandenong, having been spurned by Hawthorn and St Kilda. He won the club best and fairest in 1987, was runner-up in 1990, and named in Collingwood’s team of the century. He played 147 games. Kelly said football brought people together “from all walks of life and different backgrounds ... there are important lessons from Darren’s time at Collingwood, his life and his passing that we must continue to share with our players and staff”.

Denise Millane said while seeing her son’s No.42 retired was a great honour for the family, “we’re equally proud to see it return and be worn by a new young player each season”. “The idea that young players will have the opportunity to wear No.42 and learn about Darren’s values, his teammates and his love for Collingwood is incredibly special for our family.” Collingwood president Barry Carp said Millane held “a very special place in that [Collingwood] history and his contribution to our club will never be forgotten”. The stature of Millane at Collingwood is personified by one of the club’s most earthy coterie groups, Club 42, which was established in honour of the star wingman. In deciding to restore No.42, Collingwood sought recollections from Matthews, former football general manager Graeme Allan, teammate and close mate Denis Banks and McGuire. title: How infamous fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried missed out on a $52 billion jackpot
text:
